div.head: NO STABLES AT THE BRIDGE!
div.p: NO STABLES AT THE BRIDGE!

The Warrington Town Connell went a long way ;towards rehabilitating themselves in the eyes of the public on Tuesday night by declining, almost unanimously, to sanction Councillor COUGH'S proposals regarding the bridge. We have erected over the river the finest bridge in England. The Finance and Estate Committee had received an application to let some stables on land adjoining the river remaining upon the completion of the bridge and its approaches, and this they very wisely refused to do. Coun- cillor COUGH sought to get past the committee by coming straight to the Council, and asking them not only to let the stables, but to sell the land on which they stand. This land lying along the river 'bank from the bridge on its south-east corner—at the begq-.1- ning of Knutsford-road--is at a point that is, admittedly, the best site in Warrington for a certain class of busi- ness, and it is very valuable. It will grow in ivalue, and if the town is desirous of making money as land dealers, delay, especially as the war has brought down prices, is advisable. But we should say this site is, and will remain, priceless. Most towns have a dominant feature, as Alderman BEN NETT says—the Eiffel Tower, St Paul's Cathedral, St. George's Ball, are instances. Warrington Bridge and its surroundings—open approaches and worthy monuments—might easily be made • the feature of Warrington. At all events, we must not clog up its approaches with stables and the like. The money we owe on the bridge has to be repaid in, sixty years, and what we got for this Site would be placed to the repayments account, not credited at once against the rates, which means that we should have a contribution in relief of the rates amounting to about £lO a year. The Council emphatically declined to ,risk the disfigurement of the bridge for £lO a year. They will be poor Waringtonians if they ever agree to anything' of the kind at any price whatsoever.

div.head: MR. EDWARD PORRITT.
div.p: MR. EDWARD PORRITT.

The strength of this country rests largely with the sons and daughters she has sent forth to every corner of the world. As we have men in the Colonies and elsewhere who have rallied to the call- of the drum, so we have many eloquent tongues and pens able and anxious to champion the cause for which we stand. In another column we reproduce an address on "If the Kaiser Wins," given in the States by MT. EDWARD PORRITT, a journalist who made his debut in War- rington, and is now the well-known American correspondent on ,trade matters of the "Yorkshire Post" and the "Manchester Guardian." •As a boy, Mr. Poßturr attended People's College,' Arpley-street, in which street his mother still lives. He had a bril- liant journalistic career in this country, including Gallery experience in the House of Common. Twenty-one years ago he crossed the Atlantic, and, after doing journalistic work in various towns in the States, at last settled in Hartford, Connecticut. Married just about the time he left this country, Mr. PORRITT has a son who is at pre- sent studying at one of the big Ameri- can Universities. A brother of Mr. PORRITT'S—Mr. ARTHUR PORRITT—has also adopted journalism as his profes- sion, and is at present a member of the literary staff of "The Christian World."
It will be seen from the report of his address that Mr. PORRITT is still the greatest Briton of us all.

div.head: LARGE FAMILIES.
div.p: LARGE FAMILIES.
Should the Community Make Grants
in Aid?
A fireside discussion took place on this topic last Sunday afternoon at Academy-street Adult School.
The conference, which was arranged by the Women's Committee of the Sub-Union, was opened by

Mr. Rowland, who pointed out that though the widow and fatherless were frequently men- tioned in the Bible as being in need of care, it was assumed that a man would be able to main- tain his own offspring. But under the modern industrial system with fixed rates of wages, the, unsjcilled labourer with a large dependent family had a very big strain. The general labourer could not look for 'a higher wage in the prime of life, rit was usually possible in the case of the professional and commercial classes and to some extent among skilled artisans. Mr. Rowland produced some interesting charts representing the progress of a couple married in 1900, and showing the relative positions in 1905, 1910 and 1915. While his .wage remained sta- tionary during the whole period, the family needs steadily increased, reaching the highest point in 1915, when there might he eight dependent children. After that the children would begin to earn and the burden would de- crease. Working on the basis of estimates made both by Seebohm Rowntree in York, and Professor Bowley in Reading, Mr. Rowland estimated on a lower scale than either Rown- tree or Bo'wley for Warrington, in order to avoid anything in the nature of exaggeration. For the four periods mentioned the estimated minimum necessary expenses were 14s. 3d., 215., 275. 11d., and 365. 2d. Thus the general lab- ourer earning 225. could make both ends meet so long as he had no more than three dependent children. After that, say, from the fifth to fifteenth year of his married life, the unskilled labourer with a large family had a hard task. This was just the period of his highest physical efficiency, and therefore of his greatest worth to the community as a producer. The effects of the years of financial strain were shown in the following ways :—ln the loss of independence if helped from outside sources; in loss of education through pl'emature exemp- tion from school; in poor or inadequate food and clothing; in loss of breathing space where money was saved on house rent; and in conse- quent deterioration of health.

div.head: HOW HELP MIGHT BE GIVEN.
div.p: HOW HELP MIGHT BE GIVEN.

Charity could not, and ought not, to make good the deficiency. Advances in wages would help to solve the problem, but if wages remained at fixed rates they could not deal with extreme cases. Wages could not be based upon maxi- mum, but only upon average, needs. Something, however, might be done by making grants of, say, 2s. 6d. per head' per week for each depend- ent child over and above five. Such money could be raised by a small tax _upon juvenile adult labour. For such a scheme legislation would, of course, be needed. Mettntime em- ployers might make inquiries as to the position of their workpeople, and might even make voluntary experiments in bonuses to large families. Already generous employers, who had made grants to dependents of soldiers, had got certain useful information, and had sometim,es based their help, on the number of children, as the Government had done in regard to sep- aration allowances.

div.p: WHERE DO WE STAND?

There is certainly no reason why we and obr Allies should be dissatisfied with the state of affairs on the various fronts as revealed at the opening of the New Year. The KAISER and the EMPEROR Of AUSTRIA have been uttering platitudes about the victories their cause will achieve in the coming months, but their attitude is one of the principal. causes for rejoicing ort our side. It will have been noticed that the KAISER has abandoned his attitude of patronising familiarity with the Higher Powers, and has assumed the more seemly posture of the suppliant. That is so much to the good, as it sug- gests the idea that even the KAISER is being brought to confess that German culture has its limits. As regards our poor selves, nearly half a .year's vig- orous objection to being exterminated has convinced the Germans that we are, a force that: cannot be ignored. " Vorwarts," the German Socialist newspaper, publishes a remarkable appreciation of the British soldier, whose general efficiency, and particu- larly his skill with the rifle, it praises highly. We join in the regret of the " Vorwarts " when it speaks of "the life and death istruggle " to which two "great civilised nations with \common aims" have been "incited." \ What the KAISER thinks and what his people think are matters which do not vitally concern us just now. The 'question Is, What do we think our- selves? LORD KITCHENER acts as the collective Englishman at the present time, and his speech in the Lords on Wednesday night shows that the nation is making the effort reqpirdd by the needs of the case, and that we and our Allies are going on to assured success: We recall the message LORD KITCHENER sent to the nation in the ea:rly days when we and the French had to " back " before the fierce onslaught of ovemhelming forces of fresh Germans. He asked us to take a long view, and we should see that we were destined to grow stronger as our adversaries grew weaker. The great change from com- parative strength to weakness on their side, and from weakness to strength on ours, has effectively manifested itself. LORD KITCHENER was able to tell the country on Wednesday that "the great initial advantage" which the Germans enjoyed by reason of the numerical superiority and extensive war preparations of their Army is cer- tainly diminishing, while the Allies

are daily increasing those resources of Men and material that will enable them to _prosecute the war to a triumphant -end. That, so far as the British Army is concerned, this transition stage has been completed is clear from the last official report by "Eye Witness" at the Front. The New Year, he says, has opened upon a more favourable situa- tion for the Allies than any .they have known 'since the commencement of the campaign. So far as the British arc Concerned, the small Expeditionary Force of four divisions which took the field last August has now swelled into a great Army, which is steadily in- creasing in numbers; has become inured to war, and-can look back on a record of hard fighting such as British troops have seldom sustained in the past.

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
MERRY PANTOMIME AT THE ROYAL COURT.

This week we have pantomime at the Royal Court Theatre—a humoursome, tuneful hotch- potch; all the ingredients of real, rollicking. old-fashioned panto. compressed into the com- pass of two all-too-brief, but extremely merry- and-bright hours. And its theme is "-Cinder- ella"—" Cinderella" complete. with its win- some little kitchen-drudge, the good fairy, a real coach and pair, the immortal glass slipper, and all the rest of the concomitants of the dear old fairy story for the youngsters, and replete with the merry and not over meticulous baron, the super-abundantly ugly. sisters—who are not sisters at all, and, in fact, do not even belong to the sister sex—and all the usual droll doings and pretty girls for the grown-ups. In the hundred minutes or so during which the curtain is up one finds much to amuse, to laugh at, to tickle the ear and to feast the eye—for the little panto. has been staged in a manner which suggests that Mr. and Mrs. John Walters, who send it on tour, meant to carry through the production regardless of cost. Tudging by the hearty peals of laughter which rung from all parts of the house on the occasion of our visit, Mr. and Mrs. Walters have gathered round them just the sort of comedians that the people want, and even if they did now and then "tip us an old cuffer." we fully and freely forgave them, because of the almost entire absence of the more or less feeble war jokes and patriotic "guff" which we must confess to have antici- pated. Instead, they give us, on the whole, two full hours of harmless merriment and helped us to subscribe anew to the truth of the old adage about there being as much virtue in a hearty laugh as in many a weird brew compounded in a Chemist's whop. Yes, take our word for it, if you have not yet seen "Cinderella," hasten to do so whilst yet opportunity remains, for you will spend ,a right•jolly time and will come away feeling that you have had your money's worth cent. per cent. It only remains to say that Miss Nellie Le Breton makes a winsome Cinderella, that Mr. Julian Ross is as jolly a baron as ever had the bailiffs in; that Mr. Albert Evremond is a skittish dame of umpteen summers; that Messrs. Albert Witton and Frank Harvey are as ugly and " cattish " as the ugly sisters should he; that Miss Bessie Hargreaves is a charming Prince Charming; that Mr. Charlie T. Falla is a funny page boy as " Buttons "; that all the rest of the numerous parts are well taken, and that the chorus girls are pretty, well-trained and extravagantly costumed. If you want to know any, more• about " Cinderella " go and find/out for yourself!

div.p: KAHN° COMEDIANS AT THE HIPPODROME.

Korn° fun of the best variety is delighting large audiences at the Hippodrome this week, and patrons of this popular house will look for- ward to an early return visit of this excellent company of gifted comedians, who have scored such a success with "The Steam Laundry." Mr. Harold Wellesley leads the mirth-makers as_ "Perkins," and he makes the most of his oppor- tunities. He is ably supported by several "eccentric gentlemen," and each laughter-pro- voking situation—and there are many or them— is made the most of, to the delight of the audi- ence. Jack Walsh pays a welcome return visit, scores a " hit " with his two humorous songs, "The Ragtime Boxer" and "It's a good job I had my little candle in my hand," and, on the occasion of our visit, responded to an encore with a patriotic ditty, "There's some there from Lan- cashire." The Nelson Comedy Skating Trio perform many tricks on the "rollers," and some clever knock- about business is got through by one member of the troupe. div.head: MOTOR FIRE ENGINE.
div.p: THE MOTOR FIRE ENGINE.
Petrol Power Cheaper Than Horse
Traction.

In a report on the work of the motor fire engine for the pitst fourteen months—which re- port was laid before the members of the Town Council at their monthly meeting on Tuesday evening—the Superintendent of the Fire Bri- gade (Mr. F. H. Turner) says:— "The motor fire engine was used at ten fires and worked fourteen hours and four minutes. I estimate that the cost of petrol, oil, grease, charging accumulators, &c., for the period cov- ered by this report is £33. If the horse engine had been used at the fires attended with the motor engine, the cost of horse hire would have been £35. A striking.feature of the first year's work has been the quickness in getting away from the Fire Station and the arrival at the fire, thus ensuring promptitude in getting to work, a result which, I think, has justified the action of the Committee in purchasing a petrol engine. Good work was done by the engine at the following fires: Messrs. Ellis Vane and Co.'s -Premises, Market-place; Mr. T. E. West's Corn Store, Bridge Foot; and the St. Helens Cable Co.'s Works, where property of a considerable aniount was at stake. The engine's first-aid appliances also worked well at the fires which occurred at the premises occupied by Mr. McGrath, in Bing-street kdamage done £226, fire extinguished in four minutes), and the shop occupied by Mrs. Cox, in Sankey-street (damage done £270, fire put out in ten minutes)."

A thrilling three-reel drama, "The Pride of dennico," pictured a series of adventures be- tween the'nobility and gipsies, and many excit- ing duels were witnessed. A pretty love story formed the main theme of the plot, and all ended very happily. The staging effects of the film were splendid. The programme concluded with "Polishing Up "—one of the funniest films yet released, in which domestic squabbles played a prominent part; the breach, however, being healed.
Amongst a fine selection of dramas, comedies, and topical films which will be shown at the Kinema to-night for the last time is 2, "Bootle's Baby "—an engrossing war drama enly recently produced. -

div.head: COMFORTS FOR OUR SOLDIERS.
div.p: COMFORTS FOR OUR SOLDIERS.
CHIEF NEEDS OF TROOPS AT THE FRONT.

The military Forwarding Officer at the Oar- seas Base writes from France: "The troops generally are wanting more pipes, tobacco, laid condensed milk. They are getting a lot of cigarettes .and warm clothing, but these other things I mention are not coming out in \any quantities, and if anything could be done in this direction it would be very much appreciated by men at the front."

div.head: GLOVES AND MITTENS.
div.p: GLOVES AND MITTENS.
Splendid Local Progress With Grand
Duke Michael's Scheme.

Warrington's part in the Grand Duke Michael's Glove and Mitten Scheme is being performed as well as ever, there being a most encouraging attendance at :the Crosfield Mem- orial Hall on Tuesday evening, when the class resumed its work after a brief Christmas re- spite. Although no classes were held during this holiday, the supply of these much-needed comforts for the soldiers showed no decrease; for the employes of many. of the large Warring- ton works, which are participating in the scheme, have, of course, had more leisure time —which they very suitably -passed, in knitting for "the boys," a record thus being created. Over three thousand pairs of the coveted com- forts have now been forwarded to the Grand Duke's headquarters, to the great delight of the benefited " Tommies." Now is the time to dis- patch the gloves and mittens—when the in- tensely cold weather makes them not so much a luxury as a necessity in the tkynches.

div.head: XVOMEN LIBERAL WORKERS.
div.p: XVOMEN LIBERAL WORKERS.
Efforts of the Ladies Fully Appreciated By Warrington " Tommies."

The i Warrington Women's Liberal Associa- tion sewing meetings—for the • provision of good, warm garments for the soldiers—have this week been resumed, after a short Christmas holiday; and the steady output a- garments continues as before. The President (Mrs. A. H. Crosfield), the Secretary (Mrs. Osborne), and the other members of the committee, desire to tender their sincerest thanks to all who have so gener- ously and industriously assisted in: providing the. large consignments of garments which have already been dispatched to all parts of the home country, as well as abroad. The workers may rest assured that their services are appre- ciated to the full by the Warrington " Tom- mies"—who are not only deeply grateful for such protection against the terribly cold wea- ther' now being experienced, but who are greatly cheered in the midst of their exacting duties by the knowledge that they are not forgotten in the good old town. Continually the ladies of the class are stimu- lated to vigour even greater than .before, by the receipt' of large batches of letters. from the local "Tommies," conveying their heartfelt thanks to the workers, and expressing their appreciation of their disinterested labours. Those in the trenches, especially, have proved delighted recipients Of the gifts, for after spending long periods in the water-logged or muddy diggings, they are, of course, extremely grateful for a change of dry clothing. Garments are still required as much as ever; and the ladies of the'committee hope—and have every reason to believe—that the /supply of useful and comfortable articles for our brave men will show no decrease during the coming weeks, when such are so urgently needed.

div.head: BRIDGE SENTRIES ASSAULT POLICEMAN.
div.p: BRIDGE SENTRIES ASSAULT POLICEMAN.
A Struggle for Rifles on Walton Bridge.
CRUEL KINDNESS.

An exciting scene between two soldiers guard- ing Walton Bridge and a police officer, on New Year's night, had a .seqUel in the Stockton Heath Police .Court On Saturday morning, when, before Mr. C. Jackson Holmes (in the chair) and Mr. J. A. Ransome, Private William Keenan and Private John Jordan, of the Man- chester Special. Reserve, were charged with assaulting l'.C. Worthington. Jordan was also charged with .having been drunk. ,

SAID "GOOD-NIGHT" TO THE GIRLS. P.C. Worthington said that as he passed over the road bridge at 7.40 the previous night he saw Keenan on the Warrington side of the bridge and Jordan on the other side, leaning against the gate-post near the sentry-box. When he was bade "Good-night" by witness, Jordan answered in a drunken voice. When a young lady passed Jordan said "Good-night," and she replied. He then said .somethiig else to her, but witness could not make out what .it was. Another young lady passed and replied to Jordan's "Good-night." When she had gone on a few yards Jordan shouted after her "Come here," but she answered "No." When. Keenan came along Jordan remarked,: "I am going to ape what this policeman wants." ' ' He came up, to me," continued the officer, "and asked what I was doing there. I replied that I was going about 'my duty. He repeated his question several tiinlis and then said: `Get over that bridge.' He told me several times, bid I refused, asking him what right he had to interfere with Me.

div.head: COMMENCED TO LOAD HIS RIFLE.
div.p: COMMENCED TO LOAD HIS RIFLE.

"Prisoner then said: 'l'll show you if you won't get over the bridge,' laid commenced to load his rifle. I seized the weapon and pri- soner fell in the struggle. Keenan also held the rifle, but I succeeded in getting possession of it. Keenan asked me to give the rifle back to Jordan, but I refused. Keenan said: 'l'm his pal and I'll see if you won't give him his rifle.' Ile Stepped back •and was in the act of loading his rifle when I released Jordan and seized Keenan's rifle. I had given Jordan's rifle to a boy to take to the Ship Inn. Keenan re- fused to tell me where I could find thOsergeant.
PUSHED HIM AWAY WITH RIFLE BUTT- END.

"Prisoners went with me to the Ship Inn, where I was going to telephone for assistance. Keenan tried to regain possession of the rifle and struck me in the chest. I pushed him away with the butt-end of the rifle when he was rushing at me again. lie walked away, and I took Jordan, who was rely drunk, to the Police Station."
Superintendent Owen pointed out that Keenan's officer brought him to the Police Station.
WHISKY TO BLAME.

Jordan stated that he did not remember any- thing of the affair. A woman gave him a bottle of whisky and a man gave him a drink of beer. He then lost his senses altogether. Re left the Army with a good character after eight years' service and was sorry for what had happened. It was the first time he had been in trouble. Keenan said he was sorry, as it was his first offence. The whisky caused the trouble. A military officer said the men had an abso- lutely clean record. Perhaps the holiday had got over Ahem. The people about wee really more to blame than the soldiers, for "one brought one thing to them and another some- thing else."

PRISONERS WILL BE COURT- MARTIALLED AS WELL. Mr. 'l'. P. Bradshaw (deputy-clerk) : They will be dealt with by the military authorities what- ever is done to-day? The Officer: Certainly. The Chairman-said they were pleased to hear the men bad borne excellent diameters. The offence was such A serious one, however, that the Bench could not overlook it. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAWI JANUARY 9, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAWI JANUARY 9, 1915.
LOCAL INTELLIGENCE.
Women Liberals' Socials.

In connection with the Warrington Women's Liberal Association, an auxiliaries' social will be held in the John CrosSeld Memorial Hall on 'Monday evening, January 25th, the proceeds of which will be given to the War Sewing Fund. Whist and other games will be -played, and well-known local artistes will contribute- to a musical programme, the evening winding up with dancing.

Ward socials, at which whist, music, games and dancing will form the attractions, have been arranged as follows :—Thursday, January 21, Town Hall and Bewsey Wards; Tuesday, January 26, Whitecross; nursday, January 28, Orford; Monday, February 1, St John's; Thursday, February 4, Fairfield; Monday, Feb- ruary 8, Howley; Thursday, February 11, St. Austin's; and Monday, February 15, Latchford.

div.head: 'Warmer Week.
div.p: A 'Warmer Week.

On the whole last week was warmer than its predecessor, the Medical Officer of Health re- cording a rise in the mean temperature of four degrees. The warmest day lately was the last day of the old year, when a temperature of 47 degrees was recorded, whilst the coldest day recently was December 29th, when the temper- ature was only 30 degrees. The general direc- tion of the wind diiring the week ended Janu- ary 2nd was W.S.W., and the rainfall recorded during that period was 1.7 inch.
New Year Greetings from the Bench.

After the magistrates had taken their places at the County Sessions on Wednesday morning, Ur. F. A. Frost, who presided, said: "Before we begin this Court, I should like—on behalf of my colleagues and myself—to wish everybody in connection with the Court a happy New Year. We have certainly 'begun it in sad times; but I hope, that before this year is finished, the forces of right and justice will overcome the forces of so-called might, and that we shall have a permanent and enduring peace, and good-will among men and women."

div.head: Vicar of St. Peter's Indisposed.
div.p: Vicar of St. Peter's Indisposed.

The Vicar of St. Peter's Church (the Rev. B. Percival) should have preached his 22nd anni- versary sermons on Sunday, but owing to in- disposition was unable to do so. He sent a letter, however, which was read to the congre- gations, both morning and evening, in which he said that there were three reasons which made him feel disappointed in not being able to be with them that day. The first was that that • day had been set apart for prayers of intercession in time of war throughout the Churches of England; the second that it was the first Sunday in the New Year; and the third that it was the day upon which he should have ,preached his anniversary sermons. The doctor had, however, given him good hopes of a speedy recovery, and he (the Vicar) hoped to be able to preach his anniversary sermon next Sunday evening upon "The Motto for the Year."

div.head: Bold-street Wesleyans' New Year Social
div.p: Bold-street Wesleyans' New Year Social

In connection with the Bold-street Wesleyan Sunday School, a well-attended social was held on Friday evening of last week. The Rev. H. Williamson presided. A ,quartet, sung by the Misses Emily and Ethel Taylor and Messrs. Wilde and Page (members of the choir), opened the proceedings. A recitation was given in an effective manner by little Dorothy Lingard, and a patriotic action-song, in which the chorus "Red, white and blue" figured conspicuously, was rendered by the primary department of the Sunday School. A humorous sketch was given by Miss Smith's class, while several songs were sung in a charming manner by Miss Emily Taylor. Mr. Pearce and' Mr. Hannan gave a duet, and the former also rendered a Solo. A violin solo was effectively played by Mr. Mills, and • a rOcitation by Mr. Alfred Dutton was warmly applauded. The annual Sunday School report, presented in the form of a dialogue by twelve children, who dealt with statistics, Missionary and Bawl of Hope organisations, formed a leading feature of the programme.

div.head: £5O for Loss of a Son.
div.p: £5O for Loss of a Son.

At the Warrington County Court on Thurs- day, before his Honour Judge Qurner, the de- pendents 'of William Pugh (17), who was drowned in the Bridgwater Canal whilst work- ing for the Manchester Ship Canal Company, claimed £l5O from the Ship Canal Company, under the provisions of the Workmen's C,om- Pensation Act.—Mr. Burgis (instructed by Messrs. Chapman and Co., Manchester) ap- peared for the applicants, and Mr. Bennett (instructed by Messrs. Grundy, Kershaw and Co., Manchester), was for the defendant corn- pany.—Mr. Burgis said that whilst leading horses along the towing-path the deceased youth slipped off the canal bank into the canal and was drowned. The only question in dispute was the amount to be. paid. The defendant company said ~e5O was sufficient. Re (Mr. Butgis) submitted that the youth's average wage was 159. 4d. per week. His father earned 225. per week, and that, with the son's wages, was the whole of the money earned to maintain a family of five. The youth worked at Preston Brook, and the contention was that he would have been contributing his wages to his family for another six years if he had lived.—After the mother had been questioned with regard to what it had cost to keep her dead son, when she admitted that the amount was 14s .9d., his Honour awarded judgment for the claimants to the extent of ..250.—Mr. Bennett was allowed costs on Scale "B." There was, said Mr. Ben- nett, a trades union behind the claimants.

div.head: Brick-street Mission Tea Party.
div.p: Brick-street Mission Tea Party.

The members of the Brick-street Independent Methodist Mission held their annual New Year congregational tea party and concert on New Year's Day, in the Mission Room, a fair num- ber being present. Mr. William Barton, sen., occupied the chair, and gave a brief address, after which the Church Secretary presented his report on the spiritual and financial con- dition of the church; the Sunday School Secre- tary following with his report. Both`the re- ports were very satisfactory. At the concert which followed the following artistes appeared: Miss Marian Littlewood (soprano), Mr. W. Hopkins (humorist), and Mr. Dawson (bari- tone), with Mr. A. E. Trow as accompanist. Anthems, glees, &c., were rendered in excellent style by the Mission Choir, under the leader- ship, of Mr. Arthur Morris. A domestic farce, entitled "My Wife's Relations," was also given, the caste being as follows: Mr. Benjamin Buffins (a retired tallow chandler), Mr. H. W. Dunkley; Mrs. Buffins (his wife), Miss E. div.p: St. John Ambulance Brigade Hospital
in France.

An appeal is made locally for Thuds to equip a St.' John Ambulance Brigade Hospital in France, Mr. A. E. Spann, divisional secretary, 24, Cairo-street, acting as secretary for the pur- poses of the special effort. So rar lbout £27 has been subscribed. •

div.head: New Rifle Range.
div.p: The New Rifle Range.

The new rifle range, provided by—the Corpora- tion, will be opened by his Worship the Mayor on Thursday afternoon next. We understand that Alderman Bolton, the chairman of the Town Hall, Parks and Baths Committee, has very generously provided the rifles for use at the range.
A Collision Between Tiv. and Float.

There was a sequel to a collision between a milk float and a trap in Padgate-lane in October last at the Warrington County Court on Thurs- day, when, before his Honour Judge Gurner and a jury, Mr. Joseph Partington, tailor, Bold- street, Warrington, claimed damages in respect of the accident, from Mr. George Williams, farmer, Fearnhead.—Mr. A. Browne appeared for the plaintiff, and Mr. Madden (instructed by Mr. T. S. div.head: LovNffair Ends In Suicide.
div.p: LovNffair Ends In Suicide.

Mr. F. A. Jones held an inquest at Warring- ton yesterday touching the death of Agnes Long McLeish (29), a single woman, of 9, Slater-street, Warrington.—lt was stated that on Thursday deceased went to her sister's house at 124, Slater-street, and drank part of a bottle of lotion containing lead sublimate. She then went to the house of Mrs. Wallace, 118, Slater- street, said she had taken poison, and died on the sofa. P.C. Vose tried artificial respiration for some time, but without avail. The woman, it was stated, had enjoyed good health up to two years ago, when she had a love affair, and was afterwards confined to the asylum. She attempted to take her life last year.—" Suicide whilst of Tisound mind" was the verdict.' Liberal Worker's Funeral.

The funeral took place on Monday afternoon of Mr. Senior, of 1, Scott-street, whose death occurred on the previous Friday. The deceased, who was 58 years of age, had been ailing for about a month, and was under the care of Dr. Harold Joseph. He was a keen Liberal, and during election periods did good work for his party as a canvasser. He was very fond of bowls, and • spent much of his leisure time on the green, He was employed by Messrs. Thew- lie and Griffiths, tool makers, Mersey-street, for 21 years. By religious conviction a Congrega- tionalist, Mr. Senior worshipped at the Elm- wood-avenue Church, with which other mem- bers of his family are prominently connected. The Rev. C. P. Pitt conducted the burial ser- vice.

Warrington Photographic Society. To all the members who make or adm.iie lan- tern slides, the visit of the "Photography and Focus" box makes one of the nights of the season. This year's set is no exception, for whatever the department of photographic work —landscape, architecture, genre studies, por- traits, colour work, or scientific subjects, the selection is of the highest merit. The land- scapes with figures seemed to attract most praise, and next the portraits, one of' an old man being especially admired. A particularly fine set of scientific objects was shown—why called technical as opposed to pictorial one can hardly make out, for a slide showing three moths on the wing, another the graceful alighting of the tern at her nest, and a third a puff-ball fungus, are pictures indeed, though arranged by nature, without human inteference or "aid." A most enjoyable as well as profitable evening was spent, and a good audience was secured.

div.head: Useful Boy Scouts Entertained.
div.p: Useful Boy Scouts Entertained.

The members of the Ist Grappenhall Troop of Boy Scouts have done good work in guarding the gates of Raddon Court since it was opened as a British Red Cross Hospital. Their services were recognised on Thursday evening of last week, when they were entertained to tea and a concert by Mrs. and the Misses Broadbent, at The Hollies. Scoutmaster T. A. Edwards, three other officers and 36 boys were in attend- ance. Several. wounded British soldiers helped in the entertainment by singing songs, whilst one of them gave an encouraging address to the boys, telling them that the movement to whk.!l they belonged had done .splendid work during the war, not only in Great Britain, but also in Belgium and France. An exhibition cf wrest- ling was given after the concert by A§sistant Scoutmasters Robinson and Edwards, and at the close of the evening Honorary Scoutmaster Edwards appropriately voiced tile thanks of the guests to Mrs. and the Misses Broadbent.

div.head: Picture Treat for Poor Children.
div.p: Picture Treat for Poor Children.

At the Star Kinema, Church-street, on Friday morning, about three hundred children from the Bold-street Cripples' Guild, the Padgate Cottage Homes and the Warrington Workhouee, were. through the kindness of the management, given an enjoyable entertainment, the pictures reeled off, to the delight of the little ones, including one depicting the story of "Cinderella." Other films shown included "Bully Boy" and "Bootle's Baby," and the latest issue" of " Pathe's Animated Gazette" was also reeled off, the programme concluding with the laughable subject "A Water Dog." Portraits of General French and Admiral Jellicoe, shown between the films were vociferously cheered. On behalf of the children, who, by the way, were regaled with sweets and oranges, Mr. Dennett, a mem- ber of the Board of Guardians, expressed thanks to the management, Mr. Whitney, the manager, replying, and expressing the pleasure it gave him, and those associated with him, to have been the means of giving the children a happy hour or two.

div.head: Motorist to Pay for Killing Cow.
div.p: Motorist to Pay for Killing Cow.

At the Warrington County Courc on Thurs- day, before his Honour Judge Gurner, a claim for £l7 .was made in respect of a cow, which was killed at Thelwall on October sth by a motor car. The plaintiff was William Row- botham, cattle dealer, Agden Bridge, and tge defendant was Douglas Patterson, Knutsford- road, Latchford, whilst a third party in the case was the owner of the car, Walter Page, commission agent, Liverpool-road.—For the plaintiff, Mr. A. Browne said that the cow, with two others, was being driven along the road by a man named Livesey. Mr. Patterson was driv- ing the car, which had been lent to him by Mr. Page, and it was alleged that he rushed the car into the cow at a fearful rate near to Thelwall Church, killed the animal, and damaged the motor. Mr. Page gave Mr. PattersOn an in- demnity, and that had been accepted.—Edward Livesey said that the car was travelling at about 30 or 40 miles per hour.-Judgment for the o.incunt claimed was awarded the plaintiff, and his Honour commented c.n Mr. Page's fairness in the matter.

Suuday School Tea Parties. The annual Sunday school tea party and enter- tainment in connection with the Wycliffe Con- gregational Sunday school was held on Thurs- day evening in the schoolroom, and proved very successful. After an excellent tea had been par- taken of by the very large number who assem- bled, an entertainment was given by the scholars. During an interval, the Pastor pre- sided over the presentation of prizes. These numbered 61—an increasq of 7 over the previous year—and included 16 hotiours, 43 first-class, and 2 second-class. Mr. C. Eccles—who has recently relinquished the position of Bible Class teacher, after holding it for 18 years—handed out the prizes, and voiced his satisfaction at the in- creased number. Mr. W. Brown (superintend- ent) also made a brief speech, in which he re- ferred with pride to the large number otWyeliffe scholars who are now on active service. The various items of the entertainment were given by: The scholars of the Misses Witts', Parr's, Maybury's, Morley's, Hill's, Hawthorn's and Bateman's classes; Lilian Buck, Edith Buck, Edith Appleton, Annie Pugh, Given. Pugh, &c. —The Fairfield Girls' Sunday school also held their .annual tea party on Thursday evening, and it, too, was a big success.

div.head: TERRITORIALS' CHRISTMAS.
div.p: TERRITORIALS' CHRISTMAS.
Wealthy 'Gentleman's •Ideaster Party.
" LIVING LIKE KINGS."

Last week-we referred to the pleasant manner in which our 4th, South Lancashire Territorial Battalion had spent Christmas. Further par- ticulars to hand show that the members of the Battalion, and also of the Reserve Battalion— at stations widely apart—had an exceptionally merry and bright Yuletide, and that the people among whom they are quartered did everything they could to give them a good time; thereby showing their intense appreciatign of the pluck and sense of duty .which has prompted them to come forward and offer themselves for the ser- vice of their country. At the town in the South where the 4th 'South Lancashires are quartered, 2,500 " Tommies" sat down, in nine different buildings, to a right royal Christmas dinner as the guests of a local gentleman, and that he was no niggardly host will be gathered from the fact that each of the huge dining parties had placed before them, at his expense, roast stuffed turkey, roast beef, roast loins and legs of pork, all vegetables in season, plum puddings, mince pies and dessert; together with what Sam Weller would have called the usual liquiferous trimmings, music following the cut-and-come-again-as-many-times-as-you- like repast; for some of the best artistes in the beautiful and world-famous town gave freely of their talent, greatly to "Tommy's" delight. Not only had the generous host seen to it that the boards were well lined—he real- ised that " Tommy " is a lusty trencherman, as well as a hearty trench-man, when he gets to business—but he had also gone to the expense of seasonably decorating the halls in which he invited his guests to assemble, and, to meet them and greet them, he had arranged for the presence of a number of wounded Belgians, who are busy making recoveries in local hos- pitals,‘ so that they may once again go forth and strike a blow for their beloved and gallant little Fatherland.

Did They Enjoy Themselves? Did ihey- Did our local " Tommies" enjoy their Christ- mas? "Didn't we; not ad!" as one of them sang—at least that was the title of the song for which he was down on the post-prandial programme at one of "the banquetting halls." And,did they say "thank you!" nicely to their host and his wife? Why, they said it so thor- oughly through the medium of rousing cheers that the 'gentleman whose guests they were opined that "it said something for the builders of that they had not brought the roofs off of half of the big buildings in the place." By the way, mine host is a New Zealander— as well as being, as one guest phrased it, "a real good sort of sport "—and in a brief speech to one set of his jolly Christmas party he ex. pressed his pride at the fact that so many sons of his particular quarter of the Empire should have rallied to the Mother Country. The ex- ample of the men on the outposts of the Empire, he opined, should still further fire and enthuse those who enjoyed the inestimable privilege of living in the Motherland herself. A Right-down, Regular, Royal Time! This great Christmas party will have a place in the memories of the guests as long as they live. Officers vied with the men in making the occasion memorable and happy, and even the Brigadier himself joined in the jollity, and, at each sub-section of the monster party he called at, sang to the assembled men a rollicking old camp song, the chorus of which they took up with such gusto that the rafters rang. At as manyOf the scattered dinner parties as he 'could manage, the Chaplain (the Rev. W. Bracecamp) turned up to say grace. Oh, of a 'verity, Warrrington "Thomas" and the rest of his pals—"fra Manch, Owdham, Bowton, Widnes, Liverpool, Chowbent, and the rest of the:Lankyshire beauty spots," spent a right-ilown„ ,rggular, royal Christmas, thanks be to Mr. (we really daren't mention the gentleniah's name, for by running through the-few mi)lion names published in-the direc- tories of this country the enemy might come across it, and thus succeed in locating the whereabouts of Warrington's wiry (though not to he drawn) lads).

Christmas Day Sports 'Meeting. On the morning of Christmas Day the men held a sports meeting, at which the prize- winners included, we'll warrant you, a fair percentage of Warrington lads. Those of .the 4th South Lancashires who did not happen to be quartered in the town itself, but in a small township near by, were feted in the Parish Institute, the Parish Room, and other public buildings, as well as in private houses—where they were most-sought-after guests. They also had "a ripping time," and— save where the hospitality was privately dis- pensed—the 'cost was defrayed by public sub- scription—which shows what the people think of Private County Palatine.

div.head: IN THE NORTH.
div.p: IN THE NORTH.

In the other, and more northerly, part of the country, where Warrington warriors-in-the- making spent Yuletide, much was done to give them "the time of their lives," the attractions including a ,seFies of boxing competitions, as a sort of appetiser to the Christmas dinner.

div.head: ON THE EAST COAST.
div.p: ON THE EAST COAST.

Yet other of the Warrington " Tommies" spent their Christmas in a pleasantly-situated and pretty, town on the East Coast. According to a correspondent, their Christmas dinner was served up to them as comfortably and cheerily as if they had been partaken of at their own firesides. The Commanding Officer looked in upon them as they dined, and drank their healths, they in return pledging him and drinking to the time when they have sworn to avenge their fallen comrades. Later on they attended a concert arranged by their Captain, among the contributors to the programme being ' Captain Faulkner, Lieutenant Brunger, Lance-Corporal Lynch, and Privates Mulrooney, Larkin, Scattergood and Jolley, whilst the Japanese magician, Prince Kuroki, who was appearing at a local hall, also dropped in and gave them a clever exhibition of sleight-of-hand. A.S.C. Man Describes a Close Shave. Fraternise During Unofficial Christmas Truce.

In a letter written to his brother, 'Mr. J. Wright, of Cartwright-street, Warrington, Private Stansty Wright, of the Army Service Corps, describes a narrow escape he had from being hit whilst tending his horses near the firing line. He describes the incident thus: " I had a bit or luck the other night, as I was up the line. I was standing at my horses' heads, when one of them got shot in the foreleg. I was glad the bullet didn't hit me instead, I can tell you! I have been hicky all the way along." "Where we are, I am sorry I may not tell you," the letter continues, "but clever mind that. Suffice it to say that we are doing splen- did. We are sending the Germans back slowly but surely. We hear that they are taking 200,000 of their troops away from the front of us to oppose the Russians, so it ought to be a, bit easier for our boys. I hope the trouble will not last much longer. My word, it's a bit hot some- times, and makes you think that you won't be sorry when you are able to get out of it." The writer concludes with wishes for a happy New Year and hopes to have one for himself. Prior to enlisting Private Wright was em- ployed by Messrs. fas. Nelson and Sons, Ltd., the well-known butchers, at their Warrington branches, and he had only been twenty-one days in the Army when he was drafted to the front.

A major in the R.A.M.O writes on Christmas Day:— This has been a strange Christmas! All has been peaceful except for some occasional snip- ing on our right, but none on our front. The most extraordinary scenes took place between the trenches. In front of our bit our men and the Germans got out of their trenchel and mixed together talking, exchanging cigarettes, Lc. Some of our p_enAritually went into their trenches and stafed-ffiTre for some time, being entertained by the enemy! All joined together in a sing-song, each side taking it in turn to sing a song, and finally they ended up with " God save the King," in which the Saxons sang most heartily ! ! This is absolutely true. One of our men was given-a bottle of wine in which to drink the King's health. The Regiment actually had a football match with the Saxons, who beat them 3-2! I! These people said they would not shoot our men, but warned them against those on their (Saxon?) left. Some men of one of our regiments opposite them went out of their trenches just as the others had done, but the enemy—now thought to be Prussians— told them to go back, and firecl on them before they had regained their trenches. The Saxons and our people opposite them have arranged a sing-song for to-night, having mutually agreed not to re-open hostilities before midnight. . •

div.head: "THINGS LOOKING A BIT
div.p: "THINGS LOOKING A BIT
BRIGHTER,"
But More Men Still Wanted.
A member of the Army Service Corps, Private F. Appleton, of Padgate-lane, Warrington, who is serving at the front, writes as follows to a friend:—

"Things are looking a bit brighter out here. Lots of the refugees are returning, but, of course, they don't know whether their homes are still standing or not. Many houses and churches have been blown to atoms, and if any young man, who has no ties, could only see what the German's have done, he would not hesitate a moment about enlisting. . . "The Gurkhas do a great deal of mischief with the Germans when they make a night attack. Their officers have a job to keep them in the trenches.

"The King came through our town when he was over here, and we had to line the streets. Everyone was clean shaven, which showed our uniforms , up; but that is not thought about here. The flying machines were up above keep- ing the roads clear."

div.p: THE GALLANT ' JOCKS.'• '
Time After Time Held the Line Against
Thousands.

Driver Charles Smith, of Wellfield-street, Warrington, has sent a letter from the front (where he is serving with the Army Service Corps), in which he describes the "funny sensa- tion of being under shell fire."
He is attached to the Meerut Divisional train of the Indian Expeditionary Force, and he writes as follows:

"They are still hard at it here, and the guns are banging day and night. 'The Germans made an attack on our part of the line early this morning (Sunday, December 21st), but after a big struggle we drove them back. . . .
Letter Written Under Fire.

"it is a funny sensation being under shell fire. You can hear a shell coming, as it makes a whistling noise, which gets louder and khder, until, when the missile goes overhead, the sound is like a scream. As we drove away at least half a dozen shells went whistling over my wag- gon and burst in the field beyond. There are three bullet holes in the tarpaulin which covers my waggon—the work of German snipers. . . "A big battle is in progress here while I am writing this letter. There is one continual noise, what with the big guns, maxims and rifles.. . . We can see a farmhouse blazing in the distance. I expect it has been struck by a shell. We have orders to extinguish all camp fires, as the Ger- mans might see them and start firing on us.
Tommy Can't Understand Where the New Army Is. ,

"I think we are going to have a change out here; as instead of merely acting on the defen- sive, onr troops have begun to attack, so I expect we shall soon be moving forward. • We can't understand why some of the nAliv Army are not sent out here, as the German-a out-num- ber our men by more than four to one. There is not another regiment in the world wire -Fonld have done the work that "the Jocks "—to which I am attached—have done. Time after time they have held the line, when they have been attacked, by thousands of Germans, and it seems a shame they have to stick it."

div.head: "SNIPERS SNIPED NO MORE."
div.p: "SNIPERS SNIPED NO MORE."
NN a rri it' (on Lancer Serves in Trenches
"a la Infantry.'

Three days ago, Mr. J. Gordon, of 49, Museum- street, Warrington, received an interesting letter from his son, Corporal E. Gordon, of the 17th (Duke of Cumberland's Own) Lancers, In- dian Expeditionary Ftzrce A, who, it is interest- ing to note, recently carried off a silver cup and medal as winner of the second prize in the Indian Marathon Race, held at Sialkot (where the 17th Lancers were then stationed). The corporal is now in France, where he has been for some weeks, and writes :
"Rapid Moving."

"We have had a very busy time of it lately. On the 21st December we got sudden midnight orders to move from our quarters at B—. About noon the following day we were in fresh quarters at D—, and received orders to mount and parade at once. Then we did some rapid moving for an hour or so, eventually arriving within the fighting zone. Then we received orders to ,go in the trenches a la infantry (of course, you know we are armed with the bayonet). After a march on foot of about four miles, we arrived at our destitution (for such it was). " Swish ! But—. A brigade of our infantry just arrived in time, and we were ordered to stay in supports, just behind the trenches. My troop cased themselves in a fine old house wirii plenty of ventilation (i.e., shell holes), and tried to sleep the sleep of tired men. 'Couldn't be did!' said the German snipers; and they began to pepper us. We stuck this for about an hour, and—thanks to the bad aim of our kultured friends—we were then still smiling. Next we proposed a little stalking, and one of our French chums did the deed. Spanking! Needless to say, the snipers sniped no more.

div.head: Gallantry of the Manchesters.
div.p: Gallantry of the Manchesters.

• " I don't suppose you need any telling about the gallantry of the Manchesters the same night. We are proud of them, because they are in our force, and .of course we always say, 'Good old Lancashia:e." . . . We had a bad Christmas, but, of course, we expect that on seryic6." SNOW, FROST, RAIN AND SLEET.

Writing at the same time to his sister, Cor- poral Gordon states: "The weather has been awful lately—snow and frost, frost and rain, rain and sleet. We are all suffering from Vio- lent colds, and feel choked off altogether. . . Some of our chaps are going to receive passes to England, but I don't think I shall accept one until we have done some really good hard work. We have been under fire; in fact, the shells were dropping within 150 yards of us. Our colonel had a narrow escape with his life, us a Ger- mama sailer kail a couple a sbot4 at Aila.st .

div.head: AN EXCHANGE OF PRESENTS.
div.p: AN EXCHANGE OF PRESENTS.

Writing on Boxing Day from the trenches to his wife, a Lancashire soldier gives the follow- ing account of the exchange of Christmas greet- ings and hospitality between our troops and those of the enemy The Germans had a lot of Christmas trees lit up with candles, and our men wrote on a board, "A Merry Christmas," and the Germans wrote on another "Extreme Thanks." Then they beckoned for one of our men to go for some cigars, and he met the Germans half way be- tween the trenches. This was the Welsh Fusi- liers.. Then their officer brought a bottle of champagne, which was drunk hetween them. Then all the men came and shook hands. The Germans, having occupied a brewery, rolled two barrels of beer up to our men. There was a stoppage of war for twenty-four hours, but they are at it again this morning. The Germans were thankful for jam, &c., which our men gave them. They say their officers fire on them if they don't fire on us every time they see an English soldier.

"NOT HALF A BAD LOT, REALLY." Letter received from Private Lydall, of the London Rifle Brigade (Territorials) We had a splendid day yesterday under the circumstances. Our chaps were in the trenches, but some understanding was arrived at with the Germans, and not a shot was fired, and the 'Germans came out of their trenches, and we came out too, and met them half-way, and exchanged souvenirs and chatted, some of them knowing our lingo and some of us knowing theirs. They weren't half a bad lot, really. You would never think we were flying at one another's throats a few hours previously.

div.head: "WITH SWORD AND LA.NCE."
div.p: "WITH SWORD AND LA.NCE."
Warrington "Tommy," Though "Wait- ing," Has Many Experiences.

A few weeks ago "The Examiner" published a letter sent by Lance-Corporal C., M. Arm- strong—an old Wycliffe scholar, of , the "D" Squadron, Indian Expeditionary Force, 17th (Duke of Cumberland's Own) Lancers—to his mother, Mrs. Gordon, of 49, Museum-street, Warrington, giving a vivid description of the return journey from India to Europe. The regi- ment afterwards landed in France, and several interesting letters have since been received here from the lance-corporal. The following has just come to hand :

Sudden Order at Midnight. "France, 28th December, 1914.--I received all your Christmas gifts, and I appreciate to the full all the greetings they conveyed. I am sorry I didn't write for Christmas, but I didn't have the chance. At midnight a few days before the 20th we received a very sudden order to saddle up and turn out; and off we went up to, the trenches to hold a reserve position. The night after we took up our position, our infantry made an attack on the German trenches and a village close by; but, as we were only in reserve, we did not get into the fight. All night long, our big guns kept up a. tremendous fire; and the havoc they caused in the German line must have been awful. From where we were, we could see the shells bursting; and once, early in the night, we noticed a great flare where some part of the village had been the recipient of some considerable amount of shelling.

"Took Two Trenches and the Village." "Four of the German guns were silenced, and the infantry took two trenches and the village —a good bit of work! But what grieved us was the fact that we were not actually in it, though at the same time it was pleasing to know that our infantry could so well hold their own—and more.

"Of course, while we were there we were as infantry; for, of course, horses are no use among trenches. Well, we waited about all the following day and night, until we were relieved by fresh infantry, who went right up into the trenches.

Wounded Mars Three-Day Crawl to Safety. "On the morning after the big attack, we saw the wounded being brought to the reserve hos- pital, where they remained for ai few hours awaiting the motor ambulances which would take them away. I 'spoke to one poor chap as he lay in the ambulance. He had been wounded in both thighs three days before, and it had taken him that time to crawl back to safety. One of our fellows gave him a drop of almost boiling tea, and to show bow he must have felt he gulped it down hot as it was. The other two chaps in the ambulance with him were =con- scious. One had been, wounded in the bead, shoulders and ankles; and the other in the shoulders and arms.

"The morning we retired, all that were left of one or two regiments of infantry were re- lieved, and they gave us some very vivid tales of the fighting round that point for the previous two or three days. Of course, all this was new to us—who had not been in close proximity to the fighting before. Christmas Cheery, Though Quiet. _ _

"Somehow I fancy it will be some time before we are as close again, for, as you are no doubt aware, there is very little open fighting—both the Germans and ourselves being entrenched all along the line. However, we have been told to be patient, and that before long our chance will come to show our prowess with sword and lance. Let it come quickly, and Kaiser 'Bill' can put who he likes against us! Mind you, I am not speaking of our boys alone, but of all the cavalry who are waiting as we are. "We spent, Christmas very quietly. We had no fine Christmas dinner, of ,course; but there was plenty of plum pudding and cake—which our officers had had sent out to us. On Christ- mas Eve I received all my parcels, . . . . I can tell you I was very pleased, and am writing to thank all the senders. . . . . I am pleased to say that I am in perfect health, and not at all badly off, for we get plenty of food, &c.—in fact, we couldn't be looked after better !"

Some weeks ago, a letter sent to Prtyate George Edward Brown, of the 3rd Wercatter Regiment, of 6, Tynsley's-terrace, Bewsey-street, son of the late Inspector Brown) R.S.P.C.A., was teturned ' from the front endorsed, " Wounded and missing." "I am writing to thank you for the most thoughtful and welcome presents I received quite safely. Cream crackers and mince pies, when we are on active sex vice, are a luxury. But I knew you would not forget me.

div.head: " The Hun on the Run.'
div.p: " The Hun on the Run.'

"I have very little information to impart. We go into the trenches and get relieved, and go into billets more often than we used to. Things are easier now, and will be for a while— till we get the Huns on the run again. My word! they ran us from Mons, but it did not last long—a good job, too! I never want an- other retirement, though, in fact, they ran back quicker than we did.

div.head: German No Duffer.
div.p: The German No Duffer.

"People make a mistake when they think the German is a duffer. He is not. A lot of them are brave men; though, on the other hand, some of them don't know anything except barbarism, and have played some dirty tricks on our good old battalion. But they will not forget a com- pany of the Worcesters and Royal Inniskilling Fusiliers at —.

"Well, roll on! when I shall get a decent bed. I have not slept in one since the third of August—most of the time it has been a case of 'open-air treatment.' Roll on, Peace! . . . I hope you will all have a merry Christmas and a happy New Year. Sorry I cannot be present, as I am touring on the Continent."

div.head: CIVILIAN TRAINING CORPS.
div.p: CIVILIAN TRAINING CORPS.
Bohemian Concert to Raise Funds.
APPEAL FOR MORE RECRUITS.

A highly successful and thoroughly enjoyable Bohemian concert was held in connection with the recently-formed Warrington Civilian Train- ing Corps in the Bold-street Wesleyan School on Thursday evening. The Civilian Training Corps is an organisation quite apart from the Preparatory Training Corps, and it emanated from the National Insurance Offices. A num- ber of the young men employed in these offices felt that they wanted to do something in these days of crises, and hit upon the Idea of forming themselves, into a body -to Undergo military training so as to fit themselves for home de- fence, should the necessity arise, membership, of course, being primarily intended for those who, though otherwise eligible for enlistment in the Expeditionary Force, are, nevertheless, from various causes—home ties, &c.—unable to see their way dein' to' do so, though at the same time anxious to do something that shall be of service to their country. Once established, membership of the corps was thrown open to men in employ other than that of the State Insurance Department, and locally a hundred members were soon forthcoming, some sixty of whom have, so far, signed on under the new rules which have just come into force as the result of affiliation with the Centril Associa- tion of Volunteer Training Corps.

div.head: NAILS FOR THE COFFIN OF KAISERDOM.
div.p: NAILS FOR THE COFFIN OF KAISERDOM.

During an interval light refreshments were' served, and Lieutenant Williamson, of the 4th. (Territorial) Battalion of the South Lancashire Regiment, who is engaged locally in recruiting work, made a brief speech, in the course of which he appealed for more recruits for the fighting line. Warrington, he said, had done remarkably well in the matter of recruiting; quite as well as any other town of its size, if not better. (Applause.) But the town had not yet done all that it might; it had not yet given all of its sons that were able to come forward and offer themselves in the service of their country. There were still in this town, as in others, plenty of young men who could, and ought to, volunteer—young men who could be spared from their businesses. England was undergoing the most severe trial in her history, and it was the duty of every fit young man to come forward and do his share in crushing Baiserism, and all that they understood it to mean. (Hear, hear.) Germany was watching very keenly the recruiting that took place in England, and every man who enrolled was, so to speak, another nail driven in the coffin of Kaiserdom. For various reasons, however, lots of men felt themselves unable to enlist in the Army or the Territorials. There were home reasons, business reasons; and, in some cases, men were prevented from enlisting because they were engaged qn Government contracts. Such men, provided they were not too old, should most certainly join some civilian corps, such. as the Civilian Training Corps. Even the slightest military training would be of great service if ever the worst came to the worst, and this country had to repel an invading enemy, for it was a well-known fact that a body of men without any training—a rabble—was, to all in- tents and purposes, worse than useless. div.head: Old Lady's Fatal Fall on Christmas Day.
div.p: Old Lady's Fatal Fall on Christmas Day.

At the Stockton Heath Police Court On Wednesday afternoon, Mr. E. F. White (deputy coroner) conducted an inquiry concerning the death of Susan Jane Cole (79), who died at 22. Dedford-street, on Monday, as the indirect re- sult of a fall. Deceased was the Wife of Thomas Cole, gardener.

div.head: "Like Someone Falling."
div.p: "Like Someone Falling."

Ellen Isherwood, wife of John Isherwood, gardener, of 22, Bedford-street, said her mother (the deceased) had for the last few years been mitering irom bronchitis! On Christmas Day she was going about as usual, and at about half- past seven in the evening went upstairs. There was nobody else upstairs. Witness's father was sitting by the fire in the kitchen; her husband was talking to two friends in the‘frOnt sitting- room; and she herself had just gone down into the cellar. She then heard a noise like someone falling, and ran up to the ground floor/ - She found her mother lying at the bottom' of the stairs. At the samo time her husband came out of the sitting-room, and, picking the old Lady up, carried her into the kitchen and laid her on the sofa. Her mother said, "Mind my arm. I fell downstairs." Dr. Rutton wall sent for, and arrived about an hour afterwards. He attended deceased until her death on Monday. John Isherwood, husband of the last witness, gave corroborative evidence. Alice Maud Salmon, an unmarried nurse, of 21, Bedford-street, said she nursed Mrs. Cole until her death, and never heard her say any- thing about the happening, except that she fell downstairs.

div.head: Cause of Death.
div.p: The Cause of Death.

Dr. Hutton said that both bones of the de- ceased's left arm were broken about an inch and a half above the wrist, and there was also a wound on the elbow, but no other injuries. The cause of death was congestion of the lungs and heart failure, supervening upon the frac- ture of the forearm and the otheT injuries sus- lained by the deceased accidentally falling down- stairs.
The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the doctoi's evidence.

div.p: THE " KING " AND "QUEEN." " Crom nlng" Ceremony at Aged People's Treat.

The village "king" and "queen" this year are Mr. B. Bennett (84) and Mrs. Boddy (84), and they were "crowned," with a Smoking cap and mob cap respectively, at the annual Aged Folks' Treat, which was held in the Church .Itoom on Thursday evening. This is the big yearly function to which all the old people in the village look forward, and on Thursday there was a very happy company of the aged. Over 110 men and Women above the age of 60 years enjoyed a substantial tea, and afterwards there was an excellent entertainment given for their benefit, which was also attended by many friends and relatives.
A 34-Year-Old Festival

It is now 34 years since the treat was first organised, and with each year greater success is attained. Formerly the committee, of which Mr. J. Hallows is the very capable chairman, have collected subscriptions for the affair, but this year, owing to the war, no collection has been made, the expenses having been met out of cash in hand. • Between the tea and the entertainment Mr. S. Hallows gave an excellent lantern entertain- ment, showing old village scenes in Stockton Heath. Amongst other slides was a copy of an invitation card sent out to the old people for the treat in 1882, signed by Mr. Robert Davies and Mr. John Hallows. A picture of the first committee of the treat was also shown, the members then being Mr. Hallows, the Rev. R. P. Pearson, Mr. Calvert, and Mr. Speed, with Mr. R. Davies as leader. Mr. Owen manipu- lated the lantern.
The "Coronation."
The Rev. J. Collins presided at this year's :vat and he was supported by the Re-v. G. Curtis and members of the committee.
The Chairman said he regretted that they had to meet under the war cloud, but hoped that by the time they met again the great conflict would be over.

Performing the "crowning" ceremony in the absence of Mr. Vere B. Davie's, Mr., J. Hallows said that what they did was in recognition of the old people in the' parish, for whom they had the greatest respect. He wished the "king" and "queen" much happiness and had great pleasure in presenting Mrs. Boddy with a beau- tiful shawl, as well as her "crown." The company then joined in singing the i.tational Anthem, and the "king" and "queen" took their places on their respective "thrones," which were surmounted by the national flags. Mr. Hallows then announced that the "king" sad "queen" of last year would be presented with .2s. 6d. each.

At St. Peter's Church, Oughtrington, there was a large congregation on Sunday morning, when the Vicar (the Rev. a S. Tudor Evans) conducted a special service of intercession in time of war.

The service was attended by detachments of the Heatley Boy Scouts, under Scoutmasters Nash and Timperley, and the Home Defence Corps, the officer in charge being Mr. T. Peters. Mr. 0. G. Smith' presided at the organ. The Vicar directed the attention of his hear 4 ers to ruined Belgium and its homeless people. For the Belgians, he said, they could not do too much. Special prayers were offered, and a collection was taken on behalf of the work of the Red Cross Society, and the St. John Ambulance Brigade, the Vicar reading out two letters re- ceived from officers serving at the Front in which splendid tributes were paid to the in- estimable value of these two organisations.

div.head: SUFFERING SOLDIERS.
div.p: SUFFERING SOLDIERS.
Enulish, Irish, Seoteh and Welsh at Red Cross Hospital.

Splendid work continues to be done, among the wounded warriors, at "Brookfield "—the Lymm • Red Cross Hospital. At present there are 15 patients there, under the charge of an efficient staff of nurses—instructed by Doctors de Jong, Burrows and Thorpe, and the two resi- dent nurses, Sisters Mackay (matron) and Ilett. These fifteen include English, Irish, Scotch and Welsh soldiers, and eight of them. are .suffering from frostbite—they, with one more comrade, arriving at the hospital almost direct from the trenches just after Christmas. There were only eight " Tommies " at the in- stitution at Christmas. They had a right royal time! Aftcr the soldiers had paytaken of a splendid dinner, Mrs. Watkin and party gave an excellent entertainment, which was thor- oughly enjoyed. The following Tuesday—when their number had increased ,to 'fifteen—Mrs. Moseley, of Agden Hall, provided another en- tertainment, which was folio/wed by a supper, and was enjoyed very lunch. Last Friday night another supper was given, to the men, and proved quite as successful as its forerunners.
"Worth While Getting Wounded To Stay Here!"

Since the beginning of the work at "Brook- field," thirty-seven wounded warriors have recuperated there,. the first batch consisting of fifteen, and being followed at intervals by three others. There are three wards, each containing five beds—so that the hospital is at present filled. There are also an operating theatre and an amesthetic room. Nine operations—of minor kinds—have so far been performed, all with success. The men are loud in their praises of the treatment they receive; they are made quite comfortable, they say, • and receive, every atten- tion—in fact, "it is worth while getting wounded to stay at Btookfield,' " declared mid of their number!

"You—look sad," said Marjorie. " Sad." Peter pulled himself together. "No. I was merely thinking. I'm off on my travels again soon. I shan't be at home for next winter."
His face was brave but his heart wag lead. How happy they looked—Marjorie and his friend.

But Par rose. limping. "Take your tea, Peter," he said huskily. "One may win—and lose. Ballast tells, old boy,—and—l'm off." Peter sat down s'.owly. "He told you," he said. "He won the right." Marjorie made an elaborate pattern with cake crumbs.
"The right to—lose—" she half whis- pered. The tea room wheeled before Peter's eyes. "You mean—Marjorie—He's always won. DO you mean you like this sober old fellow best."
" I—always did—" muttered Marjorie. " And—the horse had weak hocks, Peter." "I wish to goodness—we weren't here," said Peter quietly.

The world c:eared. It was sunshine out- side, clean and sweet, yet looking down there was bitter in the cup. Pat—radiant, merry Pat—was limping slowly away. "Thank God I didn't," cried Peter, as he told her of his temptation.
"You couldn't have, she said with sim- ple trust. "And—some day—we'll make it up to Pat, Peter."
Peter, looking at his friend, wondered if they could. •
