" You see," Peter Cavanagh pulled his pipe out and looked at the grey-blue sky, 'the fact of the matter is that Marjorie cannot make up her mind whether she likes me or likes you and—we suffer." _ _

ThSipposing she likes neither," suggested Pat Fitzgerald, doutfully. "She has got to like one," said Peter stol- idly, "there's nothing to choose between ur somewhat dilapidated old places—our incomes are both singutlairly small—l believe—l really believe 'that Marjorie would take whichever asked her first, and happily ever afterwards.'" His voice shook a little as he finished, and his eyes came back from the stretch of coarse grassed, deep pool- ed bog with the purple shaded hills beyond, to his own rambling old house. Long and low and inornate as most Irish houses are, painted a cherry red, and with beds of sweet scented flowers rioting before it. At the back were acres of walled-in yards; and a huge isunny garden. Great woods sheltered the place, and a small stream came mouth- ing and gurgling right past the lawn and through the garden. - Through a gap in the trees he could see Pat's house, a grey pile, standing gauntly clear upon the craggy hill, dark pines cluster- ing round it. But there were lakes lying plac- idly at the foot of the crags. Lakes full of fish and good to boat on, and delicate shrubs which perished at Castle Cavanagh grew and flourished in the shelter by the water at Grainey. . _

Nothing to choose between their properties with a strip of fragrant scented, snipe haunted bog running in front of both houses, and beyond that the best country in the world to hunt over, rolling upwards to the towering hills. They owned half the mountain between them, the bog was shared also, the bound- aries of there demesnes touched. Peter was tall and dark and a little stolid, a studious man who read a great deal, who had been all over the world in his time, and could, as he expressed it him- self, make himself misunderstood in most languages. He shot straight, he rode a hard but quiet hunt, seldom taking anin- necessarily big fence, showing little in a slow hunt, but when hounds really ran, it would be safe to assume that Peter was with them and that it Tvould take wire itself to stop him then from keeping his place. Pat Fitzgerald was smaller, red headed, blue eyed, inexpressibly merry. His literary tastes had not got beyond Jorrocks and rosy hued weekly papers. He met life with a grin, land miisfortune, which. he deoliaied to recognise, with a. laugh of pure disdain. A pickle from his boyhood; he and Peter had been sworn friends from the day when they fished together with bent pins and unhappy impaled worms in the trickling stream at Castle Cavanagh. And it was always Pat who fell into trouble and Peter who took him out. Pat who flopped full clothed into the lake to look for a lost fish and was rescued insensible. Pat who tumbled—scoffing at warnings--ato the•, quaking bog, and was rescued, slime stifled and a:I but gone. Pat who blew off the tip of Peter's ear rabbit shooting and weeping in apology declared, he had mistaken the other boy for a rabbit. They went through school together; one quietly studious, playing in the first eleven, doing well in examinations; the other who either hit up double figures or 'went out first ball; who shirked every prep and fell into every trouble he could find, and yet was such a favourite that some means were found for pulling "Paddy Fitz" out. Now Pat was the more brilliant shot of the two; he rode young blood horses and could be seen pulling out right or left facing the blackest place, the widest ditch, the high- est stone wall. Leading unfortunate follow- ers up against wire which he was not above jumping, yet quiet Peter finished the long hunts when Pat's homes were stone cold or deep in a ditch.

Had you ,asked at Cahervally who rode the hardest, Pat's name would come on to fifty lips "Peter's a quiet chap,. rides a nice hunt but Pat—Pat's, a demon to hounds. Jumped the iron gates y'know down at Power's place —swam the Deil in floed near Bilgraney." The few who judged Peter best said little. And now love had cast a eoud upon their friendship. There had come to Ballywilliam, the half ruined horne of the Desterres, a man called Crane, who had made his millions in America and come home to the land he loved best to spend it all.

Ballywilliam's crumbling walls were reared. afresh ; the huge garden was re-stocked; pin- eries and vineries and peach houses sprang into glittering life; new slates covered the leaking roof; handsome furniture filled the big rooms, before Corncy Crane and his daughter appeared in a motor to take up their .residence in Ireland.

Marjorie Crane was a sweet-faced, bright- eyed girl, with grey eye § and fair brown hair. She took to her Irish life with the keen joy of youth, and ere three months had passed knew that Peter Cavanagh and Pat Fitzger- ald were her slaves for life. They were over every day upon. some pretext. Peter wanted to show her where the ghost walked, by the ruin- ed tower; Pat took her to the river teaching her how to throw a line. She rode fearlessly through one happy, careless winter; led over impossible places when she foll6wed Pat; see- ing good hunts more easily when Peter was her pilot; talked to them, danced with them; laughed with them through the clear spring- tide when the willows hung tassels on the banks and brown trout were to be caught in the river; drank Ireland's soft skies and winds until they were part Of her life, and now in the summer-time sometimes wondered what might happen, for things grow more serious between the two men. They watched each other lest one of them should go alone to Ballywilliam; they bought sweets and books and music for the girl as their fancy dictated. They were frank about it to each other, which saved deeper enmity; each one, acknowledging the deepness of his cause/ with no effort to cut the ground from Ulf other's feet.' "We must know soon." Peter whistled to his dogs. "We must know soon, Pat, and then, one goes away, and hey for a lifelong friendship gone down—for it would take me time. Pat, to see you married to her." "Only time, old boy. Let the right man win and there will come a day when the other will be here again—best friend as of old." Pat's voice was unusually soft. "Even Marjorie couldn't part us, Peter mine. Come to liallywilliam."

Hat& gripped hand as they started, and for a space neither spoke, for something choked their voices as they went. Out under the branching trees, where the sun flung a fret' of shade upon the thick moss, across the bog-- all white with bog cotton, fragrant with wild mint and thick flowered meadowtsweet. Deep hued, mysterious poo:s lurked- by the stacks of peat; tiny stunted bushes were aleaf on the spongy soil. Then-into the trimmer woods of Ballywilliam ; with rides cut across them, and green coated-keepers popping out to - see who intruded, and up to the stately old house which money had made young again.
-A girl, swinging in a hammock under a huge beech, raised her head as if shd expected them.
•• I knew you would come over. to cheer me she said gaily. I funked the Jevers garden party, and here I am with nothing to do. Now wasn't it nice of you not to go too?"
Pat thought," said Peter ingratiately. "you'd get a motor out and run over to see his horses training for the show—then I or. dered tea."
Here Pat announced that he had also order- ed .tea and they stared at each other desper- ately. _ _
"-Castle Cavanagh hot cakes are made of feathers," said Miss Crane decidedly. "We'll go on there. Order the motor, please. lam ready. Dad," she called—" I am going to see horses schooled."
" My dear, you I,ive for horFt-44." Crane t4ll, tau. with the Icather tanned aka

of the Co:bnial; came to his study window. He might have expected great things for his. daughter, but he seemed content to see her make her choice between the two young Irish- men, one of whom discussed books and lands and many sports with him; and the other made him laugh in his most depressed 1110- meats.

He had money enough, and he wanted hia daughter to settle close to him. The green motor came purring to the door and they slipped away along the flat bog road; then upwards by sharp turns and steep ascents to the big gates of Grainey. The car panted up the steep avenue, drawing up at the oaken door, for Grainey was built in imitation of a medieval castle, with nar- row window slits, and a huge banqueting hall and dangerous winding stone stairways. The stables were on a lower level, down long flights of steps. Here order reigned. Some ot/ the horses were still out, but four, getting ready for the Dulilin Horse Show, poked lean kindly-eyed faces from their open doors.
There were two sleek and plump and shin- ing, in dealer's condition, as Pat said proudly, and two, which were to jump, hard. er and More muscular.

They looked at Starlight and Danny, the five-year olds for sale, and then at Actress, a clean bred mare, and lastly at Simon Pure, a light 'addled, nervous looking chestnut, with St. Simon blood in him.
"He goes all right ?" asked Marjorie, watching the chestnut shrink as they saddled him.

"He'll go—for me. But if I put James up to ride him, he'll refuse and do every- thing wrong. This one of mine and Peter's Vioker ought to run each ,other close for first prize. They are both perfection." Pat had built up a course with wall, double bank and water jump, and a huge ragged wall reared by itself for competition for the championship. The horses were consistent prize winners, for he schooled them with some tricks borrowed from abroad, sheet iron in the water jump, terrifying them if they landed in; and the other fences were .child's play to Irish .hunters.

lie and Peter got up, taking their cracks round the course. Vicker fenced perfectly, if a little slowly; Simon Pure, more brilliant, would gain the clapping of the crowd. The chestnut was a hot awkward goer, one touch of his bridle setting him wild. It was pretty to see Pat, absolutely, fearless flashing round upon him, sitting perfectly still, guiding the horse with his knee more than bridle.

"You'll beat me, Pat," said Peter, getting off. "Yours is a typical show jumper. You'il beat me," he said slowly and a little sadly, for Marjorie was patting the chestnut's damp satiny neck, and Pat was smiling down at her, his boyish, merry face alight-, his little strong figure sitting easily on the fidgeting horse.

They had never resisted Pat at school. Matron, sorely tried masters, boys had all bowed to the fascination of the Irish idler. "It would be the same now," thought Peter quietly, as Pat's second horse came out to have its school. A fair performer, she was no- where following the other two. "Well, the Horse Show will decide it," said Marjorie, as they went back to the car. "Peter or Pat—will be victols then."
"The Horse Show must decide it," echoed Peter half to himself. * 71. * * * *

Clicking turnsti:es, endless rushing up of motors and other vehicles; all the sporting world to worship ling Horse in his royal state, and for the hest part of a week. Horses innumerable, pouring out of the arched entrances; prancing merrily to the rings; returning ridden by dejected owners, who vowed all judging rotten, and this par- ticular assortment only fit to decide on the merits of donkeys—kept in men smirked an. xiously, watching for the Judge's eye to be cast upon their mount. Dealers peered, lynx. eyed from the rails; Frenchmen chattered volubly, buying freely. It was a. record show even for Dublin; prices ruled high and every. thing worth looking at was being sold. Starlight and Danny, one second and one reserved, had provided their owner with funds for a winter's hunting; Peter's Merry- maid was also sold. Judging anxiously, criticising freely, Marjorie trotted from ring to ring, always—save when they had to ride their horses—with her two attendants at either side.
Pat hung upon her judgments and agreed to them all; Peter ventured quietly to con- tradict her.
"He hasn't bad hocks, hart he, Pat ?" She had fallen into the way of calling them by their Christian names as everyone else did. " Grana hocks," said Pat stoutly, kicking Peter. •
"There, you see," she said triumphantly. "I also see—the hocks," said Peter— "there out he goes." For the horse, a showy bay, came out of the ring with a string of others.

Marjorie had grown spoilt. She took it up as a grievance. "I'll buy him," she flashed and stcipped the horse with a wave of her hand. In ten minutes she returned flushed and triumphant—conscious that she had done a foolish thing and eying Peter doubtfully. "I've bought_ him, she said, "If he passes." "And if you don't fire him before this time next year, call me an idiot," said Peter cooly, braving "his love's fiery glance. After luncheon upon the second day, the two stood together at the clock waiting. for Marjorie. She had gone back to change her morning coat and skirt for the fluffy confec- tion of the jumping ring, and they were tak- ing her in. Both were in riding kit ready for the fray. The air was heavy in the central hall, heavy and hot. Peter, switching at the ground with his hunting crop, spoke suddenly. "Pat, old boy," he said nervously. " Yes—l know," said Pat. And they star- ed at each other.
"Pat, she can't make up her mind. She looks at u 4, and wonders—shall—we--toss for first chance, old man."
FirFt chance—for Marjorie. Hi) heart thun*ed as. he spoke. - -

" let- fate decide it. One must beat the other to-day, even if we don't win. Let the victor take tea with. Marjorie and— try hi A luck. It will be something to know." "Done," said Peter quietly. And Mar- jorie, radiant in something • ethereal came fluttering in. The people behind her hat were not likely to see much. Corney Crane, lean and sallow was with her. "And who—" said Marjorie as they went out into the blazing, sunshine. " will take me to tea ? Father's leaving early." " That—depends," sa:d Peter quiet:y. "I —may not be able to,"

The girl shot a (illicit glance at 'him as they passed into thp jumping enclosure. Jumping must a:ways be a little monoton- ous. But Marjorie followed it all with eager eves, and to two men taking part there was life and death beneath them at each jump. Fortune ordained that they should come out together—Vicker and Simon Pure—and both put in a faultless, loudly clapped round, 15 and 18 both numbers went up. Armagh Lad, a grey from the north, :iyau the only thing they feared. .

Out again and no judge co.ald have chosen between them. When they came in, Pat jumped off, standing in the shade of his horse—for the sun was grillinz. Next mo- ment he staggered with a cry of pain, as Oreensleeves, a hot bay mare, dealt him an accurately placed kick- straight •against his shin. Pat reeled about, groaning, Peter springing to his side. The time was approaching when they must go, out again. _ _

"No u-se, old boy. I'm in agony—ride for me," groaned Pat. "They'll call for us sep- arately now. Don't touch his head, Peter, as you love me." In the excitement of his hurt he had forgotten their compact. Peter's heart throbbed. "If Simon Pure 'id not wiu he had the right to speak." "Don't touch his head, Peter," repeated Pat.

"I'll do my best," Peter said steadily. He had not forgotten-15 and 18 to come a:one. It lay between the two. Vicker quiet and docile was yet a little bored. The steel was out of her as she fenced, without a fault, yet not with her previous Pre.

div.p: TRADE PROSPECTS IN 1975.

The Work of " Re-Constructing " Europe. With regard to the prospects for commerce and industry in 1915, everything will depend upon how soon and on what terms peace is declared (says the "Chamber of Commerce Journal "). In those industries 'engaged in meeting the requirements of the Army and Navy, work is assured until the middle or. end of the year, and even in the cotton trade it is believed that there will be a boom after the war; demand is already increasing, and a favourable feature is the plentiful supply of raw material at comparatively low prices. 'When the war comes to an end a large part of Europe will have to be reconstructed, and no country should be in a better position than the United Kingdom to undertake this work; peace will release an enormous number of vessels, thus lowering freight rates; while the dnrestricted export of a commodities from this country, the absence of heavy charges for War insurance, and a more stable financial position through- out. the world should enormously stimulate business. Altogether, our information .would seem to confirm the view recently expressed by the Chancellor of the Exchequer to the effect that after .the war there will be some four or five years of prosperity for British industries, and it must, therefore, be the aim of merchants and manufacturers to strengthen their hold on the world's markets, so as to be in the best pos- sible position to face the years of depression that must ultimately and inevitably ensue. ,

Spoonerisms. A new word has been given to the world by Prof, Spooner, of Oxford, whose affliction of unconsciously interchanging the first letters or syllables of words has performed wonders with the English language, writes Tip in the New York Press. Excited or interested while speak- ing, he made excruciatingly funny blunders that gave him a new fame. Delivering a deep lec- ture, he dramatically raised his arm, calling forth, "And Jehovah was not on the side of the kinquering congs " (conquering Kings). He convulsed a lecture hall by boldly stating that he pressed a half-warmed fish (half-formed wish) to his bosom!* Exasperated by a stupid pupil, he informed him that he had a " vreeble fit." Strictly Neutral. The account of the Local Government Board inquiry at the Town Hall the other day brought to my mind the last occasion of the kind which . I attended.. I was in good time—in fact, I was the first to arrive; and when, directly after- wards, the Town Clerk entered, I had taken a seat at the .table. .He was a newly-appointed official from another town, whs. knew not the local reporters. He evidently regarded me as a sort of enemy-alien, and could not settle down comfortably until he had satisfied himself as to my designs in relation to the citadel. He fenced a bit, and then asked me point-blank if I was there to oppose. I assured him that he had • nothing to fear from me. Still looking askance at my writing materials, he said, "Then are YOU in support?" " Well, no," I replied; " the fact is Pni neutral." " Neutral?" said he, with puzzled expression; "I really don't under- stand." So I told the new Town Clerk I was there simply as a representative of the Press. He suerced. and somehow seemed rather dis- gusted—but whether at himself or with me I could not quite determine.

• Winter Quarters. A refractory pauper committed by the Borough Justices for fourteen nays, challenged them to double the term, adding "I shall get out of the bad weather." A tramping quarry- man whom I once accorafianied along the high- way for a few miles confessed to me that he had often thus obtained food and shelter during frost, when there was nothing doing in his line. lie explained that it all began through his wife getting a judicial separation, with an order for maintenance. "I told the magistrates," he rbent on, "that I should never pay a penny, so ey gave me two' mouths. When I came out, I 11° a good tramp round, seeing the country, and working a bit here and there to keep myself going. When winter came on again, and I began to starve and feel miserable, I went back and gave myself up to the police, as I made sure there'd be a warrant out for me. So I had it /Wee and comfortable inside for another two months in th' depth o' winter. I did that for four seasons, and then th' old lass gave it up as a bad job." That sort of thing appears to be fairly common.

div.head: Children on Canal Boats.
div.p: Children on Canal Boats.

I see that the Lymm Urban District Council had this question under consideration at last week's meeting. No doubt there is still ,plenty of room for improvement, but the conditions so 'far as the floating population is concerned are altogether different from what they were when I was a young man. In those days the cabins were dirty and insanitary, whole families were huddled together, and disease was terribly prevalent. The decencies of life were impos- sible, and drunkenness and immorality were general. The children grew up without educa- tion or moral influence of any kind, and few seemed to care. Among the few were the Duke of Richmond and Gordon, and especially the late Mr. George Smith, of Coalville, who per- sistently agitated for many years, during which Period he constantly bombarded us with ap- Palling facts and statistics in support of • his demand for reform. These efforts eventuated in the passing of the Canal Boats Acts of 1877 and 1884, and gradually led to the unmistakable change for the better which the later generation has witnessed. We are authoritatively assured that many of the children are now in regular attendance at school, although it is only too true that some parents are sadly indifferent to the importance of education, and a large number of the children can neither read nor write. The school inspectors do their best, but the difficul- Iles are almost insurmOuntable, and as long as ;liildren 'are allqwed to live on the boats, it is I f ard to see how school attendance can be en- °reed. According to a recent estimate there are only about 400 children of school age now 7141 the boats. Of these, some 24 belong to the apm district, and they are receiving all pos- te attention at the hands of the responsible ota'ials. Mor r a About Coffee. 1e,,11,,ad in " Hints to Health" the paragraph "Effects of strong coffee," and I „--Zagine there are Warringtonians in the trade will not only dissent from the doctor's find- ing, but could produce lots of testimony to the direct contrary. I have before me a copy of an clid handbill issued as an advertisement when coffee Was introduced into this country, and it informed the public: that " it so closeth the orifice of the stomach and fortifieth the heat within, that it is very good to help digestion. It much quickens the spirits, and makes the heart lightsome. It is good against sore eyes, and the better if you hold. your head over it, and take in the steam that way. It suppresseth the fumes exceedingly, and is, therefore, good against headache, and will much stop any de_ fluxion of rhennis that distill from the head Upon the stomach, and so prevent and help con- sumption and the cough of the lungs. It is ex- cellent to prevent and cure the dropsy, gout, and scurvy," and so it goes on—indeed, I have not room for the long list of excellent qualities Claimed for the article. It is only right to state that these were stoutly denied, and, as on such occasions in general, some of the contest- ants contributed poetry to the controversy. Anyhow, the consumption spread, and ultim- ately, as we all know, there arose coffee-houses, .some of which became quite famous. In his "New View of London" (1708), Hatton Wrote: "I find it recorded that one James Farr, a barber, who kept the coffee-house which is nolie w Rainbow, was, in the year 1657, presented the inquest of St. Dunstan's in the West, for taaking and selling a sort of liquor called coffee, las a great nuisance and prejudice of the neigh- ,ruourhood, &c., and who would have thought 'London would over have had near 3,000 such nuisances, and coffee should have been as now So pinch drunk by the best of qualit and phy- liiciansP" Eight years or so before the publica- tion of that work, a French vivitor named 4aisson wrote: "These houses which are very numerous in London are extremely. convenient. You have all manner of news there. You have a good fire, which you may sit by as long as You please; you have a dish of coffee; you meet Your friends for the transaction of business, and all for a penny, if you don't care to spend More." As a rule, the coffee-houses were very well conducted, and. certainly one cannot say that of the taverns of the period.

The Catch of the Season. As was meet and right, that big pike which a Warringtonian took from the Gowy last April cropped up among the year's memories on the sPorts page in the last issue. It reminded me of a good old yarn which originated in the e, aPture of a pike. It is told in various ways, out this is how it is set forth in Fuller's `!. Worthies ": " A cub fox drinking out of the River Arnus in Italy, had his head seized on by a mighty pike, so that neither could free itself, and both were ingrapplied together. In this-contest a young man rolls into the water, takes them out both alive, and carrieth them to the Duke of Florence, whose palace was hard by. The por- ter would not admit him without promising of sharing his full half in what the duke should give him, to which he (hopeless otherwise of entrance) condescended; the duke highly affected with the rarity, was about giving him a good reward, which the other refused, desiring his highness would appoint one of his guard to give him a hundred lashes, that so his porter might have fifty according to his compoSition. And here my intelligence leaveth me how much farther the jest was followed."

Calendar Reform. • As I read 'Uncle Ned's "Welcome to New Year," I was somehow reminded of Mr..Pearee's Bill to reform the calendar—a measure over Which I fear it will long be difficult to arouse anything like enthusiasm, so that it will very likely find itself well in the rear of even the laggard Daylight Saving Bill. The aim is to give the last month of every quarter 31 days and the other months 30 each, and every fourth year to have a leap year day between June and Stay, New Year's Day 'being' an extra-mensuelle holiday at the end Of the year. There is an- other proposal the adoption of which would more seriously interfere with the arrangement Which we owe to Julius Cwsar. Providing like- wise for four 31-day months out of the twelve, this scheme would combine Christmas and New Year Days as one holiday on the day of the winter solstice. div.head: NEW BOOKS.
div.p: NEW BOOKS.
Political Thought in England. From Bacon to Halifax. By E. P. Gooch. (Homo University Library.) is. London: Williams and Norgate.

This is an extremely valuable book. Its importance is not to be measured by the fact that it is issued at the low price of one shilling, except in the sense that a sympathetic yet critical account of a most important epoch in our history by one of the most competent poli- tical writers of the present day is thus placed within the reach of all.

The period of thought which Mr. Gooch covers is the seventeenth century. This was pre-eminently the age of political discussion. The Reformation, as Mr. Gooch says, had broken the traditional European system in pieces, and it was necessary to erect some other structure under the shelter of which men and nations could live in safety. This -shelter was found by some in the doctrine of the divine right of kings. James. the First claimed that he, as King, was responsible to God alone for his acts, and that the people had no voice in the matter at all. And in this claim• he had the support of the Anglican clergy. .But the doctrine of divine right made few converts out- side the Anglican clergy before the Civil War. "It required the blood of Charles, the exclu- sion of his son, and the horrors of anarchy to break that passionate loyalty to the Crown which sought natural 'expression in terms of mystical devotion." Bacon was the greatest of the champions of a strong and enlightened monarchy, and Mr. Gooch gives a very clear and careful analysis of his political philosophy. Bacon's ideal was a State in which the Sover- eign, though aided by wise counsellors, should be responsible to no one for his actions within the wide and undefined limits of his preroga- tive. But, as Mr. Gooch says, his system was suited to a state of society that had already passed away. Mr. Gooch gives us the histofy of the long and bitter struggle between King and Parlia- ment for supreme power, and then between Varliament and People, culminating in the Restoration. But he selects certain of the great Men of the age for special treatment. The chapter on Hobbes is particularly full and interesting. Though Hobbes seemed to offer some support to those who held the doctrine of the absolute authority of the Sovereign, his thought never found- favour with either party in his life-time, and, as Mr. Gooch points out, it was only in the nineteenth century that his importance was grasped and the startling modernity of his cardinal principles was realised.

Interesting, also, is the account of Selden, showing how extraordinarily modern was his outlook upon life. Mr. Gooch gives a very sympathetic. analysis , of the political views of Milton, and we may quote with approval his judgment on the poet: "Milton was a prophet, not a Philosopher. No one has ever loved liberty with a nobler and more unselfish passion; but few political teachers have so little understood how it was to be obtained and defended." The analysis of Harrington's " Oceana" is very interesting, for it recalls to mind a book that is little read nowadays, although it has had an immense effect upon the modern world: The chapters dealing with "The State and Religion" and "The State and Trade" give very full accounts of powerful currents of thought that interacted with the more speci- fically political controversies of the Period.
We repeat that Mr. Gooch's book is a most valuable one, and we venture to hope that it will meet with a wide demand.

div.head: SERBIAN PEASANT.
div.p: THE SERBIAN PEASANT.

The Serbian peasant has been described as driving the plough- with one band, and shoot- ing, to keep off the enemy, with the other. Pressed between Turk and Teuton for five centuries,-he is inured to combat, the only alter- 'native to extinction of his race. The too mar- tial ' inclination reproached to the Serbian has never shown itself in aggressive action. lie has constantly beeti on the defensive, and has rarely allowed himself even just-retaliation for attack. It has come rather hard on him, accustomed to make war no oftener than once, in e decade, to have war thrust on him for three successive years, but there is no " weltschmerz " in. the Serbian trenches. Life- is taken as it comes from day to day, and a faithful reflection of Serbian optimism, resignation, pluck, resource- fulness, and determination to .win, is found in the naive missives sent home from the Serbian front—Madame. Cliristitch, in the January "Contemporary Review."

Few people could guess the date of England's first newspaper, fewer still could guess at the occasion that brought it forth. The origin of the newspaper is, indeed, hard to trace. Doubt- less Babylon and old Egypt had their news- sheets,, for one cannot imagine enlightened people living through great national doings without some official. and properly censored bulletins. But we reach the Roman period before we encounter anything that remotely suggests our modern newspaper. To Julius Caesar Rome owed the great boon of the " Acta Diurna," which, among other "Doings of the Day,' reported gladiatorial contests where a modern print describes the football match, and the notices of the plebiscita of the Comita where in latter days we look for Parliamentary notes. This sheet was written by hand and hung in conspicuous public places. According to Cicero, it gave news of trials and sentences, naval and military appointments, the decisions of magistrates, and it set an example which few later newspapers have dared to ignore in presenting a list of births, marriages and deaths.

Venice, as became its intelligence, was early in the field with a news-sheet, and incidentally bequeathed to us a title IN-Cell is with us to the Present day. The sheet was sold, and the coin which purchased it was called a gazette. The name of the coin became transferred to the print, and "Gazette" passed into several lan- guages, not least notably into our own. It was not until 1588 that England saw the issue of its first news-sheet. It was a year of great happenings, and out of the greatest of them the newspaper was. born. In using the term newspaper we must be careful not to read into it our modern meaning. The "English Mercurie," callcd after the swift-footed Greek deity, was a news-paper only in the strictest sense. The authority Cited proceeded to point out that another method would be to transfer Christmas Day and the solstice to New Year's Day. Well, of course, Christmas Day could be moved forward by a stroke of the pen. But you can't shift a solstice in so simple a manner. That could only be done by suspending the leap year rule for something like half-a-century. Every year the solstice moves forward nearly six hours; the extra day in leap year brings it back a whole day, and thus keeps it oscillating between December 21 and 22. To advance it from December 21 to New Year's Day would require forty-five years, the actual rate of gain being 5 hours 48 minutes 46 second is onnualry ; and for that long period we should have to do without a single leap year. What say my single young lady readers to this? Anyhow, the risk of such intetference is infinitesimal. Green, describing the conflict in his History, says :

!` In numbers • the two forces were strangely unequal; the English fleet counted only 80 ves- sels, against the 130 which• composed the Armada. In size of ships the disproportion was even greater. Fifty of the English vessels, in- eluding the squadron of Lord Howard, and the craft of the volunteers, were little 'bigger than yachts of the present day. Even of the thirty Queen's ships which formed its main body, there .were only four which equalled in tonnage the smallest of the Spanish galleons.' Sixty-five of these galleons formed the most formidable half of the Spanish fleet, and four galleasses, or gigantic galleys, armed with 50 guns apiece, fifty-six armed merchantmen, and twenty pin- naces% made up the rest. The Armada was pro- vided with 2,500 cannons, and a vast store of pro- visions; it had on board 8,000 seamen and 20,000 soldiers."

It should be remembered, that Philip of Spain was at this time conducting a religious war—religion, mixed with all other things—in Flanders. Ilis,army, under the Prince of Parma, was fighting in Belgium and Holland against the Prince of Orange. This was one of the con- flicts which have earned for this district the title of cockpit of Europe. The Armada, which was destroyed by "My Lord Howard" and Drake, and the wiiuls of heaven, was not the principal-invading force. The Armada was in- tended to clear the seas, then anchor at Dun- kirk, and, together with ships of all descrip- tions assembled there, embark the mixed com- pany under the Prince of Parma that were quartered at the now famous Nieuport and Dixmude. Thitehall, July 23d, 1588. Earlie this Morninge arrived a Messinger at Sir Francis Walsingham's Office, with Letters of the 22d from the Lorde High Admiral' on board the Ark-Royal, containinge the followinge material' Advices.

On the 20th of this Instant Capt. Fleming, who had beene ordered to cruize in the Chops of the Channell, for Discoverie, brought Advice into Plymouth, that he had descried the Span- ish Armado neare the Lizard, making for the Entrance of the Channel' with a favourable Gale. Though this Intelligence was not re- ceived till near foure in the Afternoone, and the Winde at that time blew hard into the Sound, yet by the indefatigable Care and Dili- gence of the Lord°. High Admiral, the Ark- Royal, with five of the largest Frigates, anchored out of the Harbour that very Eveninge. The next morninge the greatest parte of her Majesties Fleet gott out to them. They made in all about eighty Sail, divided into four Squadrons, commanded by his Lordship in Person, Sir Francis Drake rice-Admiral, and the Rear-Admirals Hawkins and Forbisher. But about one in the Afternoone, they came •in Sighte of the Spanish Armado two Leagues to the Westward of the Eddistone, sailing the form of a half-Moon, the Points whereof were seven Leagues asunder. By the best Coniputa- tion; that could be made on the sudden, (which the Prisoners have since confirmed), they can- not be fewer than one hundred and fifty Ships of all Sorts; and several' of them called Galleons and Galleasses, are of a Size nevei• seene before in our Seas, and appeare on the Surface of the Water like floatinge Castles. But the Sailors were see far from being daunted by the Nuinber and Strengthe of the Enemie, that as soon as they were discerned from the top-mast-Head, acclamations of Joy resounded through the whole Fleete. The Lord High Admirall observ- ing his generall Alacritie, after a Council of War had beene held, directed the Signall of

Battle to be hung out. We attacked the Enemy's Reare with the Advantage of the Winde : The Earl of Cumberland in the Defiance gave the first Fire: My Lord Howard himselfe was next engaged for about three Hours with Don Alphonso de Leyva in the St. Jaques, which would certaynly have struck, if she had not beetle seasonably rescued by Ango de Moncada. In the Ineane tyme, Sir Francis Drake and the two Rear-Admirals Hawkins and Forbisher, vigorously broadsided the Enemies sternmost Ships commanded by Vice-Admiral Recalde, which were forced to retreat much shattered to the maine Body of their Illeete, where the Duke de Medina himself commanded. About Sun-set we had the Pleasure of seeing this invincible Armado fill all their Sails to get away from .us. The Lord Admirall slackened his, in order to expect the Arrivall of twenty fresh Frigates, with which he intends to pursue the Enemie, whom we hope by the Grace of God to prevent from landinge one Man on Eng- lish grounde. In the Night the St. Francis Galleon, of which Don Pedro de Valdez was Captaine, fell in with Vice-Admirall Drake, who tooke her after a stout Resistance. She was disabled from keepinge up with the rest of the Flepte, by an Accident, which happened to her, of springing her Fore-maste. She carr3-cs fifty Guns and five hundred Men, both Souldiers and Mariners. The Captours found on board five thousand Golde Ducats, which they shared amongst them after bringing her into Plymouth. Such, Preparations have beene long made, by her llajestie's Wisdom and Foresighte for De- fence of the Kingdome, that (setting aside the common Accidents of War) no greate Danger is to be apprehended, though the Spaniards should lande in any Parte of it; since besides the two Campes at Tilbury and Blackheath, large Bodyes.of Militia are disposed along the Coaste under experienced Commandours, with proper Instructions howe to behave, in case a Descent cannot be prevented till a greater Force may

be drawne together, and severall of the prin- cipall of her Majesties Council and the Nobility have raised Troopes of Horse at their owne Charge, well trained and officered, which are readye to take the Fielde at an Houre's Warn- ing. The Queene was pleased to review them last weeke in the Parke at Nonsuch, and ex- pressed the highest Satisfaction at their gallant Appearance: In soe. much, that by God's Bles- singe there is no doubte but this unjust and dareing Enterprise of the .Kinge of Spayne will turne out to his everlasting Shame and Dis- honour, as all Rankes of People, without Respect of Religion, , senile resolute to defend the sacred Persone of their Sovereigne and the ,Lawes and Liberties of this Country, against all foreigne Invaders. Ostend, July 27th N.S. Nothinge is now talked of in these Partes, but the intended Invasion of England. His Highnesse the Prince of Parma' has compleated his Preparationes, of which the following ACcounte may be depended upon as exacte and authentique. The Annie designed for the Expedition is selected out of all the; Spanish Troopes in the Netherlands, and consistes of thirty thousand Foote, and eighteen hundred Horse. At Nieuport are quartered thirty Companies of Italians, ten of Walleons, and eight of Burgundians, commanded by Camp Master Generall Camillo de Monte. At Dix- muyde lie readye eighty Companies of Flemings, sixty of Spaniards, sixty of Germans, and above seven hundred fugitive English, and headed by the two Irish Arch-Traitours, the Eatles of Westmoreland, ,and Sir William Stanley. Be- sides these, four thousand Men out of the old Spanish Brigades are lodged in the Suburbes ,of Corrick, and nine hundred Reisters at Watene, together: with the Marquise de Guast, General of he Cavalrie. Volunteers of the first Qualitie are arrived from different Counc- tries, to share in the Honoure of this Enter- prize, as the Duke de Pastrana, the Alarquisse of Brisgaw, (Son to the Arch-Duke Ferdinand), Don Juan de Medicis, Don Amadeus Bastarde of Savoye, besides manic others of less note, whome we have not roome to enumerate. For the Transportation of these Forces, Vessels of all Sortes are prepared at Dunkirk, Antwetp, and Nieuport, fitted tip with all manner of Conven- iences: the flat bottomed Boates for the Caval- rie have bridges fixed to Ahem, for the more easie Shipping or Disembarkation of Horse. The Transportes. for the Foote containe each two Ovens, to bake Bread, in case they should be kepte loiter at Sea than they hope to lee. Twenty thousand . Caskes are provided at Graveling, with Nailes and Cordage, which can soone be throwne into the Forme of Bridges and a great Pile of Fascines is erected near Nieu- port, designed for the fillinge up of Ditches, covering Workemen at a Siege, and other Artes of that Nature. The little Hoyes, and Barges loaded with Arms, Powder, and Provisions, are to bee . conveyed through Canals cut from Bruges and Ghent, to Antwerp, Sluys, and Nieu- port, and soe into the British Channel!. The Scheme is Sayed to be thus settled, triat.as soone as their • great Aimado rrives in bighte of Flemish Portes, the Prince of Parma is to get out with his Transportes and joyne them. After which, they are in a Bodie to force their Waye up the River of Thames, against all Impediments, and lande as near London as they can. But whilst these Harbours are so closely watched by the united Squadrone of her Majestic and the States, commanded by the Lord Henry Seymour, it is the general Opinion, that his Highnesse will fade it impossible to put to Sea, and we hope the Lorde Admiral Howard will prevent the Spanish Navie from being in a Condition to raise the Blockade.

Says Sir Edward Grey is a Great Statesman.

An interesting address on the European War was delivered last evening by Edward Porritt at the Young Men's Hebrew Association on Win- throp-street. Mi. Porritt dealt with the war from two points; the political and the commer- cial effects on this country if the cause of the Allies should fail in the present conflict. All that the Anglo-Saxon civilisation has achieved in its fight for greater freedota is at stake, he said, in the present war, and if Ger- many should win the results of many centuries of untiring work would be completely undone. Mr. Porritt spoke of the divine rights of kings and its application to the present struggle. He showed the "history of various exponents of the system down through the ages and named the present Kaiser as a vicious illustration of the belief and what a leader who may hold such a belief may do. He may bring millions to death and ruin whole count Ties,

The struggles of the English people for greater liberty, socially, politically, and religiously, be- ginning in the .eleventh century, were portrayed at length. The net results of this great struggle for individual rights is found in three accom- plishments, namely, a freedom from serfdom, abolition of the divine rights of kings, and the riddance of aristocracy from political control. Porritt spoke of the Civil :War, and said that if the South had, been victorious in her struggle the present political freedom of Eng- land would have been set back three decades at least.

If Germany were to obtain Control o,f any or all of the countries on the side of the Allies, the United States could not continue along the lines of political and commercial history that it occu- pies to-day. The success of Germany ,vould, in fact, imperil the very existence of this country, and we would, in this event, find ourselves drawn into a conflict with Germany to defend our. civilisation just as England is being called upon to-day. In other words, the present con- flict is not, so much one of commercial rights, as it is the struggle for the existence of a civilisation—the Anglo-Saxon. Its has .frequently been said that the present conflict was one of commercial supremacy, but Mr. Porritt .emphatically: declared that this statement was by no means true. If Germany were to be victorious in the present war it would mean that the United States would face a very great restriction in her trade in the near future, and would inevitably be drawn into a conflict with that country to defend her very existence.

In connection. with Great Britain and the relation between her and her colonies Mr. Poi.- ritt said that there was More freedom there than in the United States at the present time. All of these colonies have the right to make their treaties • and to bring forward any new faritl' laws without the consent of Great Britain. In the present , war Canada will send at an early date over 100,000 men to help the mother country in the conflict, yet this action is entirely volun- tary. This fact goes to show that a greater state of freedom than now exists in these colonies would be impossible. In a word, then, if Germany should be vic- torious in the war. two conditions at least would be true; the political civilisation of not only this country, .but of all the • English speaking countries in the world would be in grave dan- ger of extermination, and, secondly, the entire commercial system of these same countries would be. completely shattered. In concluding, the speaker said, that, in his opinion, the present war would bring out Sir Edward Grey as the greatest statesman that England has had since 1.82, not excepting even Gladstone. He also said that unless the :United States were to obtain in the very near future a large export trade, that the countr)i would face financial ruin.

This New Year is so unlike tile last that we scarcely realised the departure of 1911, the fate- ful, and the advent of 1915, the hop-eful. With three and a half million Frenchmen in the field, Paris also failed to celebrate the Jour de Pan the manner of other years. " The Choco- lates, bonbons, and marrons glaces fittingly found their way into the trenches instead of into drawing-rooms. div.head: Whooping Cough
div.p: Whooping Cough

_ This disease takes from ten to fourteen days to incubate. It is contagious, and may be communicated by the breath or from the dis- charges. The onset shows itself in catarrhal symptoms, accompanied by a slight fever and cough. These symptoms continue for from seven to ten days, and are usually followed by the whooping stage. The whoop id some cases is absent, while in others the paroxysms are extremely severe and are followed by vomiting. To relieve a severe paroxysm Of coughing apply cold water to the face durin-g- th 4 attack, and give the patient nourishment immediately after the fit of coughing is over, as by so doing the food has time to digest before another attack, and weakness and complications are prevented. As in measles, the after effects of whooping cough are often very serious, the illness caus- ing extreme general debility. To guard, against the risk of complications keep the patient in a warm, well-ventilated room, and where there are bronchial symptoms keep him in bed until they disappear. Should the attack be slight the patient may go into the open air at the end of a fortnight, but it is best to confine him to the house except in the mildest weather until the whoop disappears. div.head: GOVERNMENT WHIP DEAD. Mr. Percy H. Illingworth Succumbs Jo Typhoid Fever.
div.p: GOVERNMENT WHIP DEAD. Mr. Percy H. Illingworth Succumbs Jo Typhoid Fever.

Mr. Percy Holden Illingworth; Chief Govern- ment Whip and Member for the Shipley Divi- sion of the West Riding of Yorkshire, died at his house . in Lancaster-gate, London, on Sun- day. Mr. Illingworth, who was one of the New Year Privy Councillors, had been suffering for nearly a month from typhoid fever. It was thought that he was going on well, but his con- dition became so grave on Saturday that an operation was performed- at midnight. He died 12 hours later without regaining consciousness. Mr. Illingworth was born in Bradford in 1869, the son of the late Mr. Henry Illingworth, and •came of a distinguished Liberal and Non- conformist stock. He was a grandson .of the late Sir Isaac Holden, M.P., and a. nephew of Mr. Alfred illingworth, and be followed in the footsteps of that rather rigid West Ridinc, re- 'former, first by joining the Bradford School Board, and then by securing election to the House of Commons for the Shipley Division. Educated at Rugby Sand Jesus College, Cam- bridge, he rowed in his college eight and was spare man for the University boat. 'He was, too, a fine Rugby half-back. He saw active ser- vice in South Africa as a trooper in the York- shire Hussars, and after the war was for a time a captain of the Westminster Dragoons, Im- perial Yeomanry. Mr. Illingworth unsuccessfully contested Shipley in 1900, but in 1906 the sitting Conserva- tive member found the prospect of a fight against his old opponent so unhopeful that he preferred to let the election go by default, thus handing over to Mr. Illingworth without a struggle a constituency which had been repre- sented by a Unionist for ten years. Subsequent events proved the discretion of the ex-thember, for in January, 1910, when Professor Hewina ventured to challenge Mr. Illingworth's re-elec- tion, the .Liberal candidate was returned by no fewer than 9,144 votes to 5,369. At the second. general election of 1910 Mr. Illingworth was un- opposed. One of the most popular figures hi the House of Commons, lie will be sadly mi4sed by men of all parties in an assembly which prizes most the (.I.tialities of honesty and manliness which so quickly carried Mr. 111ingworth to high office. He married,.in 1907, •a daughter of the late Mr. George Coats, cotton thread manufacturer. lie had three sons. These children Were among those rescued through the raising of the alarm by his retriever dog Trilby, from a fire at a house which Mr. Illingworth •occupied near Salisbury two years ago. .

div.head: IMPORTANCE OF THE POTATO.
div.p: IMPORTANCE OF THE POTATO.

Professor Long, in an article in "Farm and Home" on "Why Farming; Should be Inten- sive," advocates that crops should be inereaSed by means of intensive measures. If crops can be thus increased to meet war-time needs, he will live in hopes that we can permanently in- crease our crops, and so the war will have taught us a valuable lesson. There is, he goes on, no greater mistake than the supposition that wheat is the only import- ant foodstuff, and that barley and oats and potatoes can take care of themselves. All four foods are essential, and the efforts made to grow the one should be developed in, growing the others.

Far more important than most, however, is the potato, of which. we buy 3,427,000 ewts., 7,775,000 cwts. coming from Germany, France, -Holland, Denmark, Belgium and Norway. These facts are disquieting, for this means an addi- tion of 64,000 acres to our potato area if we are to obtain as many as usual. Who, with these figures staring him in the face, can fail to grow all that he cart, not only on his farm. but in the garden? The potato erop is perhaps more

easily increased than 4 grain crop by excep- tional cultivation and the ,more generous use of manure. Our average of six tons to The acre means that the best growers . obtain from eight to twenty tons, while much larger num- bers fail to obtain more than two tojour tons. It is the latter who keep down the average, and who could, if they would for once, make a serious effort for the benefit of their country as well as for themselves. Success would show them that the best work pays handsomely, • and with this proof of the fact, that work would be practised again to their lasting advantage. The potato needs dund- half a dressing of which, on deeply tilled soil, supplemented by phosphates and nitrate of soda, should secure the. crop against dry weather, and feed .it sufficiently to augment the weight of the crop. Clean land, fine tilth, a good strong variety, which is early and prolific, cannot fail to pay well, if growers who have not hitherto done full justice to the plant, will only try it. And so with our cereals; the promise of good prices should induce all growers to make the most of an opportunity which we all hope will never recur.

div.head: YEAR'S DISEASE.
div.p: A YEAR'S DISEASE.

The returns under the 'Diseases of Animals Acts. for 1914 reveal two unpleasant features, says " The Times "—a recrudescence or ,swine fever and an increase in the outbreaks of foot- and-mouth disease. The total of 4,356 cases of swine fever, compared with 2,573. in 1913, is the largest for some years back, and will have a prejudicial effect upon pig-keeping.. An aggre- gate of 27 cases of foot-and-mouth disease is not alarming, although it compares unfavourably with two in the preceding year, but the effect upon Stock raising was disproportionately great on account of the isolated nature of ,the Out- breaks both in time and locality. Anthrax also was more prevalent than, in 1913, the total being 722 outbreaks, against 594, but glanders, with a total of 97 cases, compared with 162, patasitic mange, with 1,547 cases against 2,382, and sheep seal), with 226 outbreaks against 235, all showed improvement.

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.
BULBS IN POTS.

Scores of .thousands of bulbs were plaedd in pots of soil and undrained bowls of moss-fibre in the autumn and the receptacles placed in the .dark.. It is wise, from the present onwards, to examine them weekly. When they remain too long the growth is badly weakened. With an •advance of about one inch the Tots and bowls should be brought out and gradually inured to full exposure; cover them with half :a dozen thicknesses of ordinary newspaper, and remove one daily; at the end of the,week the colour of the shoots will have changed - from yellow to green, and the more light they have after that the better they will grow. • Needless to say, they will demand more water when in the light than they did before. Bulbs in bowls are perhaps more liable to suffer from drought than others in pots. The fibre should never be allowed to get dry. .If the plants are well rooted, it is im- possible to give too much water.—“ Agricultural Economist and Horticultural Review.'

In. such gardens there is no stereotyped arrangtkaent, and a border in them, with, in the spring its maws of „snow- drops and crocusses, followed by the sweet- smelling pinks, the many varieties of bell- flower, lupins, peonies, and many other of our everyday favourites, is very beautiful. In not a few cases phloxes and Michaelmas daisies find a place, these carrying on the display far into the autumn.

Aye, truly St. Helens must have " come on" surprisingly, for Warrington have given no decided signs •of - retrogression from their early season form; and yet there is this reversal of positions! div.head: WARRINGTON'S "FLASH IN THE PAN"
div.p: WARRINGTON'S "FLASH IN THE PAN"
EFFORT.

Warrington showed signs of "bucking up" at the opening of the second half, but, alas! for the hopes of their supporters, it proved to be merely "a flash in the pan," and soon they were being driven to assume the defensive, a task at which they were kept busily engaged for nearly the whole of the rest of the game, only occasionally breaking away. The next points put up against them were registered by Durkin, who dribbled over after some excitiry, tackling work. Shallcross took the kick at goal, but failed to put the imprimatur of complete success on the effort. A short spell of play near the half-way line succeeded, and then Roberts got a-going and proved as elusive as the now almost prcreerbial Scarlet Pimpernel. Player after player did he dodge, and then, with half the Warrington pack panting unavailingly at his heels, he nipped over the line. Again did the goal kick fail, Molyneux sending the ball hopelessly wide of the mark. A few minutes later Durkin once more asserted himself, and aided by his turn of speed and his talent for trickiness, crossed over. This time the minor points came along all right, Creevey taking the kick, and sending the ball clean between the up- rights. One more try fell to St. Helens ere the game closed, Greenall doing the needful. The goal kick went astray. The final score read: St. Helens, 2 goals 7 tries (25 points); Warring- ton, nil.

div.head: HOW THE PLAYERS PLAYED.
div.p: HOW THE PLAYERS PLAYED.

There can be no gainsaying the fact that Warrington met their masters. Indeed, they outclassed in every department, and St. Helens' victory was far from being a fluke, but was, in every sense, the reward of superior ability, allied with determination. Seldom, if ever, have /the Pillmen played a better game. their forwards gave a fine exhibition of coin- 'billed play, and their three-quarters proved a (lashing quartet, whilst Molynenx was a reliable full-back, nearly always there when wanted, and wonderfully resourceful. The Warrington front rank tried hard, but, too often, their play was ix/Coherent, this want of mutual understanding causing them to bungle the all too few openings that fell to their lot. Young did his best—and a very tidy best it was—at half-back, and Laws accorded him loyal support, but it was pretty obvious that Young missed his old and tried partner, Dainteth, was' doing duty at full- back for Jolley-, who is still on the hurt list. Dainteth, by the way, worked hard in his un- wonted position, and by no means disgraced himself. Tranter was the pick of the three- qaprter line, all of whom worked hard, though units ailingly. •

div.head: LORD DERBY
div.p: LORD DERBY
Says "Enough Men Voluntarily, Or . lf •

Lord Derby, speaking at a recruiting meeting held at,Colne on Monday, said recruits had come forward in large numbers, but the ques- tion was as to whether they had, come forward in sufficient numbers. England was fighting for its existence, just as much as any of the other three' nations, and if she failed it would un- doubtedly place. us in such a position that the heel of Germany would wipe out in a few months the •freedom that had been gained in the past centuries. "Conscription is in the air," remarked his Lordship. "I have advocated national service in the past, because I wanted to see everybody trained so that when /the moment came they would be able to join voluntarily as trained men. The moment has come without that hope being realised. It is no use crying over spilt milk. We have got to see what we can do to remedy it. We may be perfectly certain that the nation as a whole is going to see this thing through, and is not going to let anything stop in the way of ,bringig it to a successful issue. We have got to get enough men voluntarily, or the country will get them in other -ways."

This occurred on New Year's Day amongst. the Y.M.C.A. players, and chiefly on that •account the kick-off did not . take place until an hour after the, time arranged. Reserves had to be chosen to make their team complete. But, as the game progressed, and playing against a very strong wind, they gave a' creditable perform- ance, and, on the whole, played better than the Mission Lads did when their turn came to play against the wind. The result was two goals against one in favour of the Mission, which just about represented the merit of the game.

Saturday's matcb was a very keen affair, for the Mission were visited by their neighbouring rivals from Newton. The latter team came with their intentions fully made up, as they had suffered defeat by the Mission earlier in the season. Both clubs were well represented and a very good game was witnessed. Macklin scored a good goal for the Cons. from a well- placed corner, and directly after Plumpton disappointed his colleagues by Missing a penalty kick. The Cons. retained their lead at the interval. The heavy condition of the ground had an effect on the players as they opened the second portion very slow in comparison to the first moiety. As the game proceeded it be- came more interesting and each side succeeded in scoring but towards the finish the Cons. had the best Of the play and the Mission goal had some narrow escapes, the final score being two goals against one, in favour of the Cons. The visitors fully deserved their victory and were well served by Macklin, Lawrance and Rhu- bottam, whilst on the home side Massey had more opportunities to show his abilities than his confrere, and Griffiths and F. gaton also played well.

Paddington were at home again and were visited by the St. Barnabas' eleven. The latter were well represented and included Darlington and Midge, former members of the Great Sankey team, and H. Challinor, of Fairfield, whilst the home lot had their usual eleven, with the exception of Chamberlain.. A keen and interesting game was witnessed by the spec- tators, and, as the score indicates, the visitors were the better .team, the result being 2-0 in their favour, a goal being scored in each half. The visitors' li-111f-back line proved too good for the home team and continually upset their attempts at combination, and Darlington, Illidge and' Vernon were good in the forward line, the two latter scoring the goals. For the home team Harrison kept a good goal, and Holmes was the best back, and Taylor; at centre-half, did well. Bramhall and Garnett were the pick of the forwards.

There was a good attendance at West-avenue to witness the game between the "Heathens" and Cadishead Wesleyans, in. the North Che- shire League. The latter team, at the present time, head the table. The visitors brought their strongest eleven and the game was keenly contested, the "Heathens" leading- at the interval by the odd goal. The second half was a repetition of th, first, and it was only by the last kick of the match that the fisitors equal- ised. The goal was scored from a corner-kick. A shot being sent in, Hooper caught the ball and the referee judged him as having gone over the line with the ball in his possession. It was a disappointment to the home team to have to share the points, but at the same time they may cpngratulate themselves as being the only team up to the present time that have taken two points from the Cadishead team. .

Elmwood Congregationalists at last are be- ginning to assert themselves, for last week, when they- were opposed by the Central, and after being in arrears at the interval, they suc- ceeded in winning the game by two goals against one, this being the " Cons.' " third victory.
PADDINGTON v. ST. BARNABAS'.
On Saturday the above teams met at Padding- ton.

Paddington: Harrison; Smith and E. Holmes; Spencer, J. Taylor and J. Holmes; Wainwright, Bramhall. Darbyshire, Taylor and W. Garnett. St. Barnabas' : Davenport; Jefferson and E. Long; O'Neil, P. Challinor and H. Challinor; Darlington, Oakley, Illidge, D. Vernon and Barratt.

The ‘! Saints" won the toss and Taylor started against a stiff breeze. The home team were soon in the visitors' goal area, where Long relieved finely. Darlington, gaining the ball, raced away and centred finely from near the corner-flag, the ball coming to Midge in front of goal, but he was neatly robbed by 'Holmes, who kicked away, and then Wainwright and Darbyshire took play to the visitors" end, but they failed to get past the defence of Jefferson and Long. A free-kick given against Brain- hail was taken by H. Challinor, who placed nicely to Midge, and the latter got the better of the home 'backs and sent the leather past Har- rison, registering the first goal for the visitors. The home team now made efforts to redeem this reverse, but the visitors' half-backs intercepted many well-timed passes, and upset the attempts at combination, and Spencer worked the ball down towards the "Saints" goal, but Darby- shire failed to accept the opening. Half-time : St. Barnabas', 1 goal; Paddington, nil. _ _ _

The home team improved in the second half and*Bramhall sent in a good shot, which Daven- port cleared at the second attempt at the ex- pense of a corner, and this was not improved upon. Then O'Neil placed to Darlington, and from his centre Illidge fell 'on the ball. Holmes relieved, and H. Challinor secured the ball and passed to Vernon, who scored the " Saints' " second goal. The home team now tried to pull themselves together to reduce the arrears, but the visitors' half-backs proved, too good. Darby- shire broke away and Long canceded a corner. This was well placed, but a foul by Taylor against Illidge spoiled the chance of the home team. Result St. Barnabas', 2 goals; Pad- dington, nil.

div.head: ELMWOOD CONS. V. WARRINGTON CENTRAL
div.p: ELMWOOD CONS. V. WARRINGTON CENTRAL

The above teams met at Manchester-road. Elmwbod Cons.: Holt; Joe Phoenix and J. Mellor; Pritchard, Ashton and Hall; Clayton, W. Phoenix, Kendrick, Wells and Smith. Central: Williams; 'Glover and Ashcroft; Williams, Brown and Erason ; Farrell, Kennedy, Holmes, Hands and Longshaw. Referee, Mr. G. Knight. The Central won the toss and played with a strong wind in their favour. During the first ten minutes the game was evenly contested, and then the visitors, with the aid of the wind, made an attack on the home goal, which was stubbornly met by Phcenix and Mellor. The pressure was relieved by Ashton sending out to Clayton on the right, where a good oppor- tunity <if scoring was. wasted. Brown, for the Central, placed Kennedy in possession, and the latter forced Phcenix to concede a corner. This was well placed, and the ball was sent out by Hall and was obtained by Longshaw, who promptly returned and opened the score for the visitors after twenty minutes' play. Encour- aged by this success, the visitors played more keenly, and again attempted to lower the home citadel, but Ashton was in one of his 'best moods and upset the opponents' efforts. Mellor had to concede another corner, which was cleared. Half-time: Central, 1 goal; Elmwood Cons.; 0.

On resuming, it was the turn of the Cons, to play, with the wind, and they soon made their presence known near the Central goal, and from a free-kick Ashton skimmed the bar. This brought temporary relief to the defence, but the home half-backs were on the alert and Hall placed to Wells, who transferred to W. Phoenix, and the equalising goal was secured. It was now a tug-of-war and both teams played stren- uously, the visitors being repeatedly pulled up for offside. They adopted the kick-and-rush style, but Mellor and. Phoenix defeated their efforts to score. A.s the end was approaching, the Cons. gained the upper hand and attacked the visitors' goal very strongly, when, Williams failing to clear properly_ a long shot from Ash- ton, Kendrick rushed in and gained the 4 lead for the Cons. The home team had other op- portunities, which they -failed to accept, and the result was :—Elmwood Cons., 2 goals; Central, 1 goal. ,

STOCKTON HEATH v. CADISHEAD WESLEYANS.

'The above teams met at West-avenue, Stock- ton Heath, on Saturday, before a good-sized crowd of spectators. As this match was of great importance to the visitors, they brought their strongest team, and the "Heathens" were also well represented. The home captain 'won the toss and took ad- vantage of the wind and sun. The home team at once set a good pace and early became aggressive. Thompson, smartly checked an advance by Vernon and Lloyd, and, directly afterwards, Smith forced Barker to concede a corner. The visitors then paid a isit to the home end, but Hooper and his backs were equal to their task, and, as the game proceeded, the visitors' defence was severely thud, and Noden and Barlow, of the "Heathens" middle line,' were very prominent. The consistent form of the "Heathens" met with its reward,. when. after twenty minutes' play, Smith beat Barker with a splendid shot. Following this reverse. the visitors played more strenuously, and Cornock and Lowe showed smart combination, but Taylor, who was playing an _effective game at centre-half; equalised for the visitors, and half-time arrived with the score at one goal each.

On the resumption, the .game was very evenly contested, the respective 'defences showing up well under pressure. Lloyd, Vernon , and Smith, for the "Heathens," were consistent in their play, while •Cornock and Lowe proved dangerous opponents to the home defenee. Fol- lowing, some good combined efforts by the "Heathens'" forwards, Lloyd .succeeded in gaining the lead for the /home team thirty minutes after the change of ends.. The Visitors " put all in" to get on equal terms, and close on time they gained a corner-kick. The ball was dropped well in front of the • goal and Blooper, in stopping a shot, was adjudged by the referee to have allowed the ball to go over the line. The visitors thus equalised. No fur- ther scoring took place, the result being a draw of two goals each.

IVounded.

At the Borough Police out on Wednesday, before Mr. J. W. Hayward (in the chair), Alder- man Smethurst, Mr. C. Jackson Holmes and Mr. W. T. Williams, Private George Allen was charged with being an absentee from the 3rd Battalion South Lancashire Regiment, stationed at Sefton.
P.C. Yates said he received information from prisoner's wife, and when he saw prisoner he admitted that he had been absent since Janu- ary 2nd.
Prisoner: I was going back last night, but the wife called in the policeman.

Supt. Williamson: They all say that, your Worships. The Chairman; I am pleased to see that your wife has some regard for the King and country at this time. Such men as you are badly wanted to-day. You will be handed over to an escort.

div.head: Father-in-Law's Offer To See Him Back.
div.p: Father-in-Law's Offer To See Him Back.

Prisoner's father-in-law, who is an Army pen- sioner, asked if he could take the prisoner back to his station. He was a thorough good man, and it was the first time he had been brought before a justice of the peace. He (the spOaker) was prepared to pay all the expenses, and he would see him to the headquarters and report to the police when he had done that. Supt. Williamson pointed out that the police were responsible for the man now that he had been arrested.
The Clerk: Why didn't you take him back before?

The Father-in-law: I took him to the railway station, and I thought he would be all right. Ile has been to the war and received a wound, and I suppose he came up to see his wife and children. Being an old pensioner, I could not tolerate him coming away without leave. The Chairman: We are pleased to see the in- terest you are taking in the case, but we are of the opinion that he will have to be handed over to the escort.

div.head: DRUNKEN ABSENTEE.
div.p: A DRUNKEN ABSENTEE.

At the Police 'Court on Tuesday, John Nixon was charged with having been drunk in. Arpley- street and also with being an absentee from the Manchester Special Reserve, stationed at Moore. Supt. Williamson said that prisoner arrived at the Police Station the previous night, and said he wanted to join his regiment at Cork. A communication•was received from the guard of the Ship Canal with reference to the mans Prisoner said he had leave for a day, but when he went back he saw another man at his' post, and went away again. The Chairman (Mr. W. Hayward): I sup- pose drink is at the bottom of it. The mistaken kindness of friends.
Supt. Williamson said his friend was going to Cork, and in his drunken state he thought he was going as well. He was ordered to be Winded over to an escort.

div.head: RECRUITING Booli.
div.p: RECRUITING Booli.
New Year Marked By Increased Number of Lymm " Tommies."

Now that the Christmas and New Year festivi- ties are concluded, the young men of Lymm have answered the call of King and country right nobly, and, although Lymm had already sup- plied a surprisingly large number of her young and strong for the defence of justice and the right, no less than thirty more have this week been enrolled.

Interviewed by "The Examiner" representa- tive, the Lymm recruiting officer expressed the opinion, that this increase, is due, not alone to the conclusion of the annual merry-makings, but also to the householders' census. What- ever the cause, however, great credit is due to the village for so splendid a recruiting total.

div.head: RELIEF FUNDS.
div.p: RELIEF FUNDS.
Lymm's Magnificent Response to the
Various Appeals.

Not only has the village of Lymm given prac- tically all its young men either to the Army or Navy, but it has also responded magnificently to the various appeals made on behalf of the relief funds. Since the collections for the "Beechwood" (Belgian Refugees') Fund were commenced on October 28th, several hundred pounds have been subscribed—the amount for the first ten weeks alone totalling £5OO. This becomes all the more surprising when it is recollected that the Lymm distfict contribu- tions to the National Relief Fund exceed £lOO, and that the local*, Red Cross Funds have not gone lacking in any way.

div.head: " BEECHWOOD " BANQUET. Committee Members Entertain Belgians Right Royally.
div.p: " BEECHWOOD " BANQUET. Committee Members Entertain Belgians Right Royally.

The Belgian Refugees residing at " Beech- wood " will long remember last Saturday even- ing, for upon it the members of the committee entertained them in a regal manner, having subscribed a handsothe amount specially for the purpose of a banquet, which, to use the expression of one who attended, was "tip-top." About forty sat down to dinner, each being handed a beautiful and suitably worded menu- card, decorated with the flags of the Allies, and presented by the treasurer, as a souvenir of the occasion. As to the dinner itself—a glance down the menu would render further conviction as to its excellence unnecessary; it was a credit to the ladies who had arranged it. During the repast the bell-ringers of the Lymm Parish Church gave several melodious selections upon the handbells.

After dinner, an enjoyable concert was given by. the following artistes: Misses Molesworth and H. Watkin (both of whom rendered solos in French), and Miss Brundrett (one of whose songs was also translated into that language, earning loud applause); Messrs. Harry Pearson, H. E. Odber and H. E. Gibbon; Mr. Buckle (of Manchester, who completely mystified his audi- ence numbering a hundred—with his mar- vellous conjuring); and the Oughtrington Boy Scouts (who performed excellently upon the handbells). Mr. 0. G. Smith accompanied all the solos upon the piano; and Mr. Alfred Wat- kin (chairman of the Lymm and District Com- mittee), who presided over the concert, made a brief speech, in the course of whieh he said that much credit was due to all the ladies and gen- tlemen who had carried through the arrange- "lents so successfully. The many artistes also deserved their thanks. (Applause.) The concert was followed by refreshments, of which the whole company partook. Dancing was then indulged in until midnight, proving a great attraction.

The Social Committee, which made all the arrangements, consisted of: Mr. W. N. Moles- worth (chairman), Mesdames T. F. W. Dixon, A. Watson, and Dorling (matron); Miss Alul- lard; Messrs. T. Nash and Owen Davies; and the officials were: Messrs. W. Afttllard, H. T. Mercer and T. F. W. Dixon (hon. treasurer). Out or the same fund as provided the dinner, each Belgian at "Beechwood" has been pre- sented with a useful and valuable Christmas present.

div.head: "GIVE ME MY WAGES."
div.p: "GIVE ME MY WAGES."
Threats to Threshinu Machine Owner.
SMART FINE:*

At the Police Court on Monday, John Russell, 172, Knutsford-road, was charged with wilfully breaking two panes of glass, vallied at 3s. 6d., at the workshop of Walter Fitter, in Liverpool- road; with having used threats to Fitter, and also with having been drunk in Liverpool-road. Walter Fitter, threshing machine owner, 36, Hood-lane, said that on Saturday morning pris- oner should have been with some other men at Stretton baling hay. Instead, he turned up at the works in Liverpool-road in a drunken and quarrelsome condition. He fell out with the other men, with the result that they all gave up work, and the job on which they were en- gaged had to stop. Prisoner demanded his money and he (witness) said: "You are not in a condition to receive it." Prisoner then% said, "I will punch your . . • in, and put a knife in you."
Prisoner (whose head was bandaged): He is telling lit,q !
Said He Would Set the Tackle Afire.

Witness: He threatened me with his 'fists. I said to him: "I will not give you your money," because I did not know what was due to him. He said he would see that the tackle did not work on Monday, as he would set it on fire. There was a crash then, and I saw that he had smashed the windows by throwing a pair of tongs through them. I then sent for a police- man, and prisoner cursed and threatened all the time we were waiting for the officer. Pris- oner also started threatening my son, and in defending himself, my son lifted a piece of, iron up, and it caught prisoner's face. Prisoner acted like a mad man.
Prisoner: His son deliberately struck me. I was not drunk.
Dan Fitter. the son, said he had the iron in his hand, and when prisoner attempted to strike him he lifted his hand up to guard himself. He had no intention of striking prisoner.
