The Town Council on Tuesday gave their sanction to a proposal put forward by the Finance and Estate Committee to replace the unsightly hoarding in front of the land in Legh-street, belonging to the Corporation, with a wall to be built of old dressed bricks.

div.head: MORE BELGIAN GUESTS.
div.p: MORE BELGIAN GUESTS.
Bank Quay Mission as Hosts to a Family of Seven.
A TOUCHING RE-UNION.

Happy recollections, of Warrington will be especially treasured by at least nine of the refugees from Belgium, • for it was in our good old town, yesterday, that, after many anxious months, there was a joyous family re-union. Two Belgian sisters living at Hall Nook, Pen- keth, have -spent many weeks wondering what had become of their widowed sister and her family. Words ' are altogether inadequate to express the joy and pleasure they "must have experienced when the news that their sister, with her two married daughters, three grand- children, and a daughter-in-law, were coming to live in the town. The meeting .on Bank Quay Station yesterday afternoon mage a very. touching scene. As the 4.41 train steamed in the sisters' eyes eagerly scanned the carriages until one of the familiar faces was seen, and then, with uncontrollable tears of joy, hand., were gripped and hot, eager kisses were ex- changed between the happy women.

div.head: WELCOMED TO THEIR NEW HOME.
div.p: WELCOMED TO THEIR NEW HOME.

The party were then conveyed in cabs to 35, Golborne-street, where they will be the guests of the Bank Quay Working Men's Mission, who have furnished the house and undertaken to maintain the seven refugees. Mr. Tilling, the secretary of the Mission, along with the Matron from Hall Nook, met the party at the station, and on arrival at Golborne-street the refugees were welcomed by members of the Mission Ladies' Committee, who have done such useful work, along with the Mayoress, Mr. G. Dale (vice-president of the Mission), Mr. Fair- hurst (borough treasurer), Mr. T. Dale, Mrs. E. Osborne, and others. "The Examiner" representative was informed that the husbands of the daughters and daughter-in-law were now fighting at the Front, and that the women had been fortunate enough to see and speak to them at Calais after their flight from Malines, through Duffel, Ghent, Ostend, Nieuport, Fumes and Dunkirk. They had been at Droit- wich for about eight weeks, and words could not express how glad they were to meet their relatives.

INDISSOLUBLE TIES OF FRIENDSHIP. Mr. G. Dale (whose speech was translated to the Belgians in their native tongue by the Matron of Hall Nook) said he extended a hearty welcome to the refugees on behalf of the Mis- sion. Whilst they deplored deeply the sad and tragic circumstances which had separated the refugees from their own people and native land for a time, they were glad to think that they could render them some little service, and at- tempt to lessen their suffering. "Our admira- tion for you and your fellow-countrymen who are fighting side by side with the British and French soldiers is very great, continued Mr. Dale, "because we know they are fighting for the triumph of freedom, truth and righteoUs- ness, and we have not the slightest, doubt about the result. We believe the principles of justice and integrity will be vindicated. In the meantime we shall spare no pains in our endeavours to make you feel quite at -home amongst us, and we hope when you return to your beloved Belgium you will experience ten- der recollections of your association with our people, and that you will carry lute* the fact that your heroic nation is bound to ours with cords of hope, truth, honour and affection, which no mere military power can break asunder. (Applause.)
Mr. Fairhurst also welcomed the refugees on behalf of the town.

"It is wonderful what you are, doing for us. This house is much too nice for us; and we can- not yet realise it is for us." This Wag-the-reply we got when we asked -what thelii3elgians thought of the hospitality of the Warrington friends at the Bank Quay Working Men's Mission.

div.head: WHEAT PRICES RISING.
div.p: WHEAT PRICES RISING.
Highest _ Figure For Years At This
Week's Local Market.

As was only to be expected, in view of the total stoppage of the Russian wheat supply to this country, coupled with the added cost of Canadian grain necessitated by the heavy rates of insurance, &c., consequent upon the war, wheat still continues to advance in price. At the Warrington Market on Wednesday the ab- 'normal price of 7s. per 701 b. was reached. This is the highest price at which wheat has sold locally for many years, and ,there is every likeli- hood of still further advances as time goes on. At Wednesday's market oats ruled firm at 3s. 91d. to 3s. 11d. per 451 b. Wheat and oat straw were in better demand and sold at from 235. to 255. per ton, free on rail. XX flour fetched 40s. per 2801 b. and best bran is. sd. per , 201 b.

div.head: BREAD DEARER.
div.p: BREAD DEARER.

On Monday the price of bread went up—as decided upon by the Warrington and District Master Bakers' Association—qnd best bread now costs 70. per 41b. loaf and seconds bread 61d. Since August last, when the war broke out, flour has advanced nearly lls, per sack, which is equal to an increased cost of over lid. on every 41b. loaf. The immediate result in the rise of price has been, as might be expected, an in- creased demand for seconds bread among the working class, and the confectioners, we are informed, have already begun to feel the pinch; in fact, our representative was informed by one

tradesman, who does a large business in fancy 14king, that already there has been such a drop in the demand for the grade of article in which he specialises that he contemplates a reduction in his staff.

div.head: WELL DONE, WARRINGTON!
div.p: WELL DONE, WARRINGTON!

There has been a great boom in recruiting this week, as was anticipated would he the case after the holidays. No less than 353 of War- rington's sons have answered their country's call and enlisted at the Police Station. About 150 have joined the Royal Field Artillery, and 38 have' joined the South Lancashire Regiment; in fact, recruits have enlisted in all the branches of the Army these last few days, and Warrington can feel that a good week's work has been done.

div.head: FOR WOUNDED WARRIORS.
div.p: FOR WOUNDED WARRIORS.

Another Pound Day is announced to be held in connection with the Raddon Court Red Cross Hospital for wounded soldiers on Thurs- day of next week—January 25th. div.head: ST. JAMES' MEN FOR THE FRONT.
div.p: ST. JAMES' MEN FOR THE FRONT.

The Vicar of St. James', Latchford, has com- piled a list of 241 names or parishioners who are serving with the colours or on our battle- ships. div.head: SOLDIER'S TRIBUTE TO WYCLIFFE.
div.p: SOLDIER'S TRIBUTE TO WYCLIFFE.

• Recently we 'told how the Wycliffe Congrega- tional Church workers had forwarded forty-five Christmas parcels to their soldier and sailor members in various parts of the world. Of many of these the receipt has now been acknow- ledged in terms of delight. Writing to his parents this week from near the firing line, a trooper mentions the various Christmas gifts he has received, and continues: "I have written to Mr. James to-day, so that he can thank every- body at Wycliffe for me. Theirs was a splendid parcel. It seems strange that they should have thought of some of the things they sent—such as ointment, bootlaces, de. Splendid'!"

THE CUSTOMS AND TOMMY'S " TOBACCO Parcels containing articles such as tobacco, cigarettes, &c., addressed to British troops abroad are not exempt from Customs charges in the country of destination, except in the case of parcels of tobacco, cigarettes, &c., for the Expeditionary Force on the Continent of Europe. Senders of parcels for the Expedition- ary Force serving out of Europe may, however, undertake at the time of posting, the payment of the Customs and other charges, ordinarily payable by the addressees, under the arrange- ment set forth on pages 64 and 65 of the current Post Office Guide, particulars of which may be obtained on inquiry, at any Post Office.

div.head: PHILOMATHS ABANDON ANNUAL DINNER.
div.p: PHILOMATHS ABANDON ANNUAL DINNER.

In view of the war the committee of the Warrington Philomathic Society haye decided to abandon their annual dinner thisiyear, and they feel sure that they will have the concur- rence of the members in the step they have taken. As hitherto, collections will be made at the forthcoming meetings of the Society on be- half of the local Soldiers' Tobacco Fund, and members who desire to contribute, but are un- able to attend the meetings, should forward their contributions to the Hon. Treasurer. Al- ready the society has sent the sum of .12,2 14s. to the Mayor for the purpose of swelling the fund, to say nothing of a large quantity of cigarettes given by various members.

TWO BROTHERS WITH THE FORCES. During the last few days Mr. and Mrs. E. Lloyd. of 140, Evelyn-street, have beard news of 2 of their 4 sons, who are at present serving their country by land or sea. Stoker Edward Lloyd, a Naval Reservist, the parents have ascertained, is at present interned in Holland. How he comes to be there is not known, but it is probable that he formed one of the Naval Brigade Which helped in the defen e of Ant- werp and afterwards crossed the Dutch fron- tier. Stoker Lloyd was twelve years in the Navy, and before being called up with the Reserve he worked for Messrs. Cammell, Laird and Co., of Birkenhead. The other son, of whom the parents have had word, is Private Harry Lloyd, who joined the Royal Field Artiitery shortly after the outbreak of war, and who was twice wounded, his hurts on the last occasion having been treated in a French hospital.. Ha- ving once again made a satisfactory recovery, he is now back in thS firing line.

div.head: GALLANT TAR THANKS YOUTHFUL GIFTMAKER.
div.p: GALLANT TAR THANKS YOUTHFUL GIFTMAKER.

Miss May Drinkwater, of 14, Priestley-street, Warrington, was one of the many young ladies in the town who responded to the appeal for Christmas gifts for "Jack" and "Tommy." With her gift she enclosed a card of greeting, which bore her name and address. 11-4 r present found its way to one of the gallant lads serving aboard H.M.S. Jupiter, viz., Seaman T. L. Wil- liams (24 Mess), and, in acknowledgment; he has forwarded the youthful donor the following letter :—" Dear Miss May,—l take the greatest of pleasure in writing you these few lines to let you know I received your kind and most generous gift, for which I must thank you very much. We are all happy here, under the cir- cumstances, and are doing our best to bring this grim struggle to a successful issue. I wish you a Happy and Prosperous. New Year, and hope that your path through life be smooth and pleasant."

div.head: CAME OVER WITH THE CANADIANS.
div.p: CAME OVER WITH THE CANADIANS.
Transferred to the Inniskillings and Was killed.

News has been received in Warrington, by Mrs. Elwood, of Parker-street, of the death Of her brother-in-law, Private Williai Duncan, of the Inuiskilling Fusiliers, who was fatally hit on November 7th last. Private Duncan saw service as a Volunteer in the South African War, and upon his return from that campaign, was, together with a number of his comrades, feted by the people and honoured by the Cor- poration of the little Irish town, of which he is a native. Some few years ago he migrated to Canada, when lie was successful in obtaining a good post in one of the largest dry-goods stores in the Province. A young than of considerable ability and: sterling character, it was not long before he was promoted to a position of great trust, and he was, as the phrase goes, "doing splendid" when the call came for Canadian volunteers. He at once offered himself and was accepted and drafted over to England. Upon arrival at Salisbury Plain he applied to be per- mitted to exchange into his old regiment, the Inniskillings, and, his request being granted, he went out to the Front with them a few weeks before he met his death.

Mr. Duncan was married in Winnipeg about three years 'ago, and he and his bride spent their honeymoon in touring Ireland, England and the Continent, en route spending several clays with. Mrs. Duncan's sister, and her hus- band, who were then resident in Sheerness. It may be of interest to mention that, by his marriage, Mr. Duncan was related to the late Mr. Graham Gilmour, the intrepid young aviator, who met his death, in tragic fashion, some two years ago.

div.head: [ALL RIGHTS RESER.VED.I
div.p: [ALL RIGHTS RESER.VED.I
THE DECAYING ART ‘OF FORGERY. ,

Forgery is one of the decaying arts. Every year athe criminal records give less space to the fate of unsuccessful penmen. If the the- ory of statistical progression could be abso- lutely relied upon it would be safe to pro- phesy that within the coming twenty years forgery will be as rare as gold sweating, highwaymanship and other obsolete crimes.

div.head: A. FIFTY TO ONE CHANCE.
div.p: A. FIFTY TO ONE CHANCE.

It is to be hoped that the advance of educa- tion has had much to do with this desirable change, but it is more than probable that the main contributing cause is the increase in the obstacles to successful forgery. Slowly but surely the arts and sciences have bee q en- listed and applied to circumvent the Ague; and to-day one is almost tempted to feel that Me man who perpetrates a successful forgery is entitled to credit for his witoundiug in- genuity. At the most. modest computation the odds against a forged monetary document go- ing through without detection are something like fifty to one. Even when successful, the criminal generally owes as much to fortuitous accident, commonly called luck, as to his own skill and cunning. In other words the cheque or bill- is cashed not merely because the pen- man has imitated the signature so skilfully, but rather becaut4e he was able to present the paper under conditions momentarily favour- able. The forgery of the signature is not the principal part of the plot. There are numer- ous other cogs in the wheel of circumstance, and it is usually the breaking of one of them that brings detection and disaster.

div.head: PROTECTIVE METHODS.
div.p: PROTECTIVE METHODS.

It would obviously not be for the public benefit to reveal the secrets of the detection machinery. Let it suffice to say that there are scores of protective methods known and used by bankers and professional dealers in valuable documents, of which the average criminal, actual and prospective, can • know nothing. So well are these secrets preserved that it has often happened that the convicted forger has never learned the true means of his detection. The chemist has been responsible for the killing of a once common and potent form of cheque fraud,--which oddly enough, could not be strictly termed forgery for the reason that the signature was untouched. The meth- od adopted by the thief was to obtain by le- giitim'atie if underhand means from the in- tended victim a genuine cheque for a small amount. By the application of certain chemi- cals the amount written in and the figures were removed, and a larger amount, with the name of another payee substituted. The sig- nature was left. 'Many thousands of pounds were obtained by this method until the chem- ist, was called in to devise 'an ink for cheque printing which would defy all eftorts at al- teration.
